Gen Studio makes game assets on your own computer, on one GPU: concept art, 3D models, rigs, animation, textures, effects, shaders, sound, music, voices, text, anime art and pixel art. The results go into your Godot project. It's for people making a game alone or in a small team, who want every asset to keep a record of how it was made.

Learn by doing. The path goes from first launch to a small scene in Godot, about two hours in all; each part ends with something you made and takes 10 to 20 minutes.

You define an anime character once, take shots of her, then make a visual novel sprite set and a 2D rig for Godot. Noa, the alchemist on these pages, was made this way. About 30 minutes without her own LoRA. Training one adds 20 to 40 minutes.

documents.t: You set Gen Studio up, learn where things are in the window, and make one picture: the concept art of a market cart, with two takes to choose from. About 10 minutes, plus the downloads, which run in the background.
You make a brass lantern: concept art, a 3D model, a game mesh inside your target look's budget, and then the file in a Godot project. About 15 minutes, most of it waiting for the models.

You export everything from the earlier tutorials in one go, add the Gen Studio dock to the Godot editor, and build a small scene: the courier walking on a cobbled street beside a lantern, a pond, a blue flame, with the theme playing. About 15 minutes.
You film yourself doing a move and put it on your character as a clip. About 5 minutes, plus the filming.

You turn on the pixel pack and make a small retro set: a potion sprite, a knight, a key icon, a sheet of meadow tiles, an overworld tune and a coin sound. The pictures are true pixels on a limited palette, not a big picture made to look blocky. About 15 minutes.
You describe a shader in a sentence and get a .gdshader that compiles in Godot, with sliders for what you want to tweak. Then you read the judge's notes and steer a retake. About 5 minutes.

You give the village its sound: two sound effects with variants, a looping theme, and a waltz written note by note that you can edit bar by bar. Then you clean one sound up and run it through effects. About 15 minutes.

You make three things that aren't models: a cobblestone texture that tiles, with its maps and a Godot material; a pond-water shader that Godot compiles; and a blue flame as an animated flipbook. About 15 minutes.
You design a voice for the village's potion seller, write a haggling scene as a dialogue file for Godot, write an item's text, and then have the scene spoken line by line. About 10 minutes.

You make one plain body, dress it in pieces that fit over each other, save them as an outfit, and swap outfits at runtime in Godot. About 60 minutes for the body and four pieces. Most of that is the model and rig steps, which run without you.
documents.s: A base body and an outfit

documents.t: You do what the earlier tutorials did without the window: one asset from a terminal, a file of jobs that runs overnight, and an agent that makes, looks and picks for you. About 15 minutes at the keyboard. The batch runs while you're away.

Gen Studio makes game assets on your own computer, on one GPU: concept art, 3D models, rigs, animation, textures, effects, shaders, sound, music, voices, text, anime art and pixel art. The results go into your Godot project. It's for people making a game alone or in a small team, who want every asset to keep a record of how it was made. Generation runs on your machine. The network is used to download models and to search free asset libraries. What you need: Linux and an NVIDIA GPU (built and tested on an RTX 4090 with 24 GB; many steps want 16 to 24 GB of graphics memory), 80 GB of disk for the Minimal install, 266 GB for Recommended or 358 GB for Full, Godot 4.7, and Blender on your PATH. The details are in Set up Gen Studio.

How does a piece of clothing end up fitting one character and moving with it? A wearable is a piece of armour, clothing or an accessory made for one rigged character or base body. It comes out as its own game-ready mesh that fits the body and follows every clip.

No open model builds a garment onto a given body mesh. What does work: image models are good at "the same character, now wearing X", multiview 3D models build a mesh from fixed views, and fitting a mesh to a body and copying skin weights can be done with plain, tested code. So a wearable is made in ordinary steps, each with takes: Design, Mesh, Fit, an optional Paint, and Skin.
documents.s: Why not generate the piece in 3D directly?

documents.t: The sample project has a character, the courier, and a wearable made for her: "a wide-brimmed felt courier hat with a feather". Design. The courier is rendered in her rest pose from the front, left, back and right. The hat is drawn onto the front view first, then onto the others with the finished front as a reference, so all four show the same hat. The hat is cut out of each view by its description, and the four cut-outs are checked against each other in 3D. A view that disagrees is redrawn. The step stops here for your review. Mesh. The Route field picks how the piece is built. A piece that hugs the body (boots, gloves, shirts) is made from the body's own surface, so it fits by construction. A piece that stands off it, like a helmet or this hat, is built in 3D from the four cut-outs. A cape is its back-view outline hung behind the body. On Auto the route is chosen for you; set it yourself if the take comes out wrong. Fit. The hat is placed where its cut-outs say, hugged onto the head without losing its shape, then pushed out to the Clearance so the head can't poke through. Skin. Each point of the hat copies the skin weights of the closest point of the courier's body where distance and direction agree, and the rest are filled in smoothly. It's exported on her skeleton, so it follows every clip she has. As a check she's posed (arms up, knees bent, a twist) and any body points that poke through are counted.
A piece on a higher Layer (a coat, 2) is fitted over the same character's pieces on lower layers (a shirt, 1). One piece per Slot and layer is worn at a time.

Capes, skirts, long hair and tails should swing. Gen Studio doesn't bake a cloth simulation into the clips. It adds bone chains down the parts that hang, and Godot's SpringBoneSimulator3D swings them while the game runs, so the cloth reacts to whatever the character does, not only to the clips you made. Which part hangs comes from the Cloth field, or on Auto from the piece's words (cape, skirt, coat, robe, scarf). How it swings comes from Cloth material: cloth, leather, hair or chain. A character's own long hair gets the same treatment on its Rig step. Before a Skin take is kept, Godot swings the chains without a window. If they stretch more than 5 %, the take fails and says so.
documents.s: Cloth: bone chains, swung by Godot

documents.t: A wearable belongs to one body. Make it again for another character. The character needs its Rig before you make a piece for it. Describe one piece at a time: "leather boots", not a whole outfit. Make lower layers first, so the coat is fitted over the shirt. If a piece pokes through, raise Clearance and retake. Design takes a few minutes at any profile: four views are drawn one after another.

Where do the steps and models come from, and why can you switch them off?

Gen Studio's core owns the queue, the VRAM scheduler, the asset folders and the settings. Every step that makes something comes from an extension, also called a pack: a folder with a gen-extension.toml that lists its steps, what each profile runs, its form fields, and its model files pinned by exact revision and hash. The app reads that file without running any of the extension's code, so it can list a pack's steps, sizes and licences before anything is installed. A pack can also bring asset kinds. Turn it off and its kinds, steps and downloads go away. Assets you made with it keep their folders, and come back when you turn it on.

The sample project's potion is a pixel sprite. That kind comes from gen.pixel, which ships off. Until you switch it on in Settings → Extensions and restart, New asset has no pixel kinds at all. The anime shots are the same story with gen.anime. The festival waltz comes from gen.composer, which is on by default and needs no model.
documents.s: An example: the potion and the pixel pack

documents.t: Models are research code, and they pin different, conflicting versions of the same libraries. One shared Python environment would break each time a model was added. So a pack that brings its own model code runs it in a worker: a separate process with its own environment under the data folder, installed by gen install workers. The core talks to it over a small protocol and passes file paths, never the pictures themselves. Three things follow. A crashed worker can't take the app down. Stopping the process frees all its VRAM. And adding a pack can't break one you already use. Many packs need no worker of their own. They run on the managed ComfyUI, with workflow templates pinned by hash, or on the managed llama.cpp server for text.
documents.s: Why each worker has its own environment

documents.t: An add-on is an extension that offers another model for its parent's steps. The step then shows a Model choice beside Profile. It's on only while its parent is on. A Kit is smaller than an extension: an optional recipe for one step, made of a kit.toml, a guide and a preview picture. It names a model family Gen Studio already has and holds no code, so installing one runs nothing. Without a Kit a step runs on Default. A library is where model files and environments live. The data folder is the home library. You can add libraries on other drives and place a pack's models there. Gen Studio links them back into the data folder, so every step finds its files in one place. If a drive is missing, the step says which one and nothing is written to the empty mount point.

Turn off packs you don't use to keep New asset and Settings → Models short. Turning one off deletes nothing. A switch applies when you restart the app. Models take the space, not the packs. Put the big ones on another drive with a library. A pack's models can download the first time a step needs them, after the app asks. gen update writes the installed pins to gen.lock, and gen restore installs exactly those on another machine. You can write your own pack. gen new extension scaffolds one and gen ext validate checks it.

Why are there two quality settings, and which one do you change? Two separate settings shape every result. The target look is the era your game looks like. The profile is how long a step may take. Keeping them apart means the same models serve a PS1-style game and a PS4-style one, and you can try ideas quickly and finish them slowly without changing the look. The app says target look. The CLI, gen-project.toml and meta.json say fidelity. They're the same thing.

PS1, PS2, PS3 or PS4, set once per project (Settings → Project → Target look). It sets the budgets: Target look Prop triangles Character triangles Texture Clips PS1 800 1,000 256 px 15 fps, stepped PS2 4,000 4,000 512 px 30 fps PS3 6,000 10,000 1024 px 30 fps PS4 50,000 30,000 2048 px the clip's own rate It also sets the sound's sample rate, the palettes of low-fi textures and the preview shader. It mostly changes the finishing: reducing the mesh, baking, palettes, frame rates. Those are plain code, not models, so they're quick and give the same result every time.

Ultra fast, Fast, Balanced or Quality. The profile picks the model and its settings, and it can swap the model entirely. The profile is decided in layers: the project's Default profile, then a per-step setting in gen-project.toml, then the Profile field of the take you make. If a step has no recipe at the profile you ask for (Rig has none at Balanced), it runs the next lighter one it has, and the take records that.
documents.s: Profile: how long a step may take

documents.t: The sample project's lantern was made at Balanced. Its Concept ran FLUX.3 klein at 16 steps. At Fast the same step runs Z-Image-Turbo at 8 steps, and at Quality Qwen-Image 2.1 at 1280 px. Its Game mesh at Balanced is a Blender decimate and bake; at Quality it's MeshAnything V2. None of that changes how big the lantern is in your game. In a PS1 project it comes out at 800 triangles with a 256 px texture, in a PS4 project at up to 50,000 with a 2048 px one, at any profile. The lantern can also break the project's rule. The Game mesh step has its own Triangle budget, Texture size and Normal map fields, so one hero prop can carry more detail than the rest. The value used is recorded in the take.

Pick the target look once, from the game you're making. Change it per step only for exceptions. Explore at Fast. Retake the keepers at Balanced or Quality: the takes sit side by side to compare. Balanced and Quality often need models the Recommended install leaves out. The app asks before it downloads one. Some pairs make little sense, and the app warns but lets you run them. PS4 at Ultra fast bakes normal maps from a rough mesh. PS1 at Quality is slow for a budget of 800 triangles. A step that runs out of GPU memory goes again one profile lighter and says so on the take.

How is an asset put together, and what happens to the rest when you change one part of it?

An asset is one thing you make, and it's a folder in the project: assets/courier/. Its kind (prop, character, music, anime shot) decides the steps it starts with. A prop starts as Concept, Prepped cut-out, Mesh, Game mesh. A character is Concept, Turnaround, High poly, Game mesh, Rig. Some steps are optional and wait for you to start them: Paint and Frame in 3D on a model, Clean up and Effects on a sound. Each step takes the result of the step before it and makes the next thing. Steps connect by what they pass on (a picture, a mesh, a rig, a clip, a sound, text), not by which model made it. That's why a profile can swap the model behind a step and the next step still works. Every run of a step makes a take. One take per step is in use, and that's the one the next step builds from. The takes page covers what a take holds.
documents.s: An asset is a row of steps

documents.t: The kind gives an asset its first steps, but the list is the asset's own, written in its asset.json: each step, and the step it comes after. So you can add a step to the end of a row with the dashed +, and two assets of one kind can end up with different steps.
documents.s: The step list belongs to the asset

documents.t: A path (a branch) starts from any step of the first row and runs beside it, with its own steps and takes. The app names them b1, b2, and you can rename them. A character's clips work the same way: each clip is a row of its own that starts from the Rig. Take the courier from the sample project. Her first row ends at Rig. You want to try a hand-painted texture without losing the baked one, so you branch from Game mesh and add Paint: that's b1/paint. Then you add a walk: that's clips/walk/motion, built on her Rig. Three rows, one asset, and nothing on the first row changed.
documents.s: Paths: another route from the same step

documents.t: Every take records its parents: the takes that were in use on the step before it when it ran. Use a different take of the courier's Turnaround, and her High poly, Game mesh and Rig were all built from the old one. They're stale. The b1 Paint and the walk come after those steps, so they need to run again too. Stale isn't an error and nothing is lost. It means "this doesn't match what you chose any more". Run the steps again and they match. Use the old take again and nothing is stale. Some steps stop for a review before the rest runs, so a long chain doesn't build on something you haven't looked at: a character's Rig, a sound or a track after its first step, text before it's translated.
documents.s: Stale: built from something you no longer use

documents.t: You can change your mind at any step. The cost is running the steps after it again, not starting over. Try a different finish on a path, and keep both. Export refuses an asset with stale steps, so Godot never gets a rig from one mesh and a texture from another. Deleting a step takes the steps after it, and the paths and clips leaving from them, to the project's .trash/ folder. The first step can't be deleted. On the command line a step goes by its id: Game mesh is retopo, Rig is skin, a branch step is b1/paint.

What happens to a result when you make another one, and how can any result be made again?

Every time a step runs, it writes a new folder. That's a take. The app calls it Take 2, the folder is v002: <project>/assets/lantern/steps/concept/v001/ v002/ steps/retopo/v001/ One take per step is in use. Which one is written in the asset's canonical.json. The other takes stay where they are, so you can go back at any time. Using a different take changes one line in that file and moves nothing. The first take of a step is used straight away. A take you make later, with Retake, New take or gen retake, is kept beside it and not used until you choose it with Use this take or gen promote.

The sample project's lantern is a prop: Concept, Prepped cut-out, Mesh, Game mesh. All four ran from the first concept. You retake the Concept with "blue glass panes" moved to the front of the prompt, like Take 2 better, and use it. The cut-out, the mesh and the game mesh were built from Take 1. Each take records its parents, the takes in use on the step before it when it ran, so the app knows they no longer match. They're stale (dashed in the diagram). Re-run stale, or gen rerun-stale lantern, makes a new take of each from the takes now in use, in order. If you go back to Concept Take 1 instead, nothing is stale any more. A take built on another take of the same step (Build on Take 2, on Retouch or Edit) records that take's parents, since that's where its picture came from. Re-run stale leaves such a take marked for you to rebuild by hand.

Each take folder has its outputs (concept.png, high.glb, low.glb, sfx.ogg) and a meta.json with the fully resolved job: the step, the profile and the target look it ran at, and any fallback to a lighter profile; the model, its extension and worker versions, and its weights pinned to a full 40-character Hugging Face revision; for ComfyUI steps, the workflow template's sha256 and the ComfyUI and custom-node commits; every value of the step's form, the seed, and the rewritten prompt if you asked for one; the parent takes; timings, and the licence of the model and of any imported file. Where the file format allows, the job is also embedded in the output itself (PNG text chunks, glTF extras), so a file you drag out of the folder keeps its history. This record is the take's provenance. gen run --from <meta.json> re-resolves a take's job from it and checks that it comes out the same. A seed alone wouldn't do that: the same seed with another model revision or a changed workflow gives a different picture. If a result can't be remade from its meta.json, that's a bug.
gen.db is an index of jobs and assets that makes the app fast. The folders are the source of truth. gen doctor --reindex rebuilds the index from them.

Retake freely. A new take never replaces the one in use until you say so. Compare takes of one step side by side, then use the one you like. Stale steps are a to-do, not a loss. Export refuses a stale asset until they've run. Discard… and Reroll move takes to the project's .trash/ folder. Gen Studio doesn't empty it. You do, when you're sure. You can copy a project folder to another machine and every take and choice comes with it. meta.json doubles as a credits log: the licence of every model and imported file your game uses.

How do image, 3D, motion, sound and text models share one graphics card? Most of these models want most of the card, so they take turns. The scheduler decides what is loaded, when it's swapped out, and what happens when something doesn't fit.

Every model runs in its own process: a model worker, the managed ComfyUI, or the managed llama.cpp server. Each declares how much VRAM it needs and how long it may sit idle before it's unloaded (5 minutes is typical). When a job needs a model that isn't loaded, the scheduler unloads the others that can't share the card, then reads the real free VRAM from the driver before it starts the new one. Declared numbers are only a starting point. The queue row says what's happening ("waiting for 21 GB of free VRAM"), so a swap never looks like a hang. While a step runs, Gen Studio samples how much memory its own processes hold. The peak of the last five runs is kept per step and profile, on your machine. After a step has run once, the fit badges and the scheduler use that measured number.
documents.s: One heavy model at a time

documents.t: The sample project was made by one batch file: eight anime shots, a handful of props and characters, sounds, music and text. The queue prefers the job whose step ran last, so the eight shots run back to back with their model loaded once. When the lantern's Mesh comes up, the scheduler unloads the picture model, checks the free VRAM and loads the 3D one. The text jobs go to llama.cpp the same way. Nobody had to order the file by model.
documents.s: An example: the sample project's batch

documents.t: A step that runs out of GPU memory is queued again one profile lighter: Quality, Balanced, Fast, Ultra fast. The take records each fallback, with the reason. If free VRAM stays too low to start at all, the scheduler waits a short while, then fails with how much it needed and how much was free. Games, browsers and other AI tools use VRAM too. The scheduler names them in a warning ("other programs are using the GPU: pid 4321 (3.2 GB)") and never stops a process it didn't start.

Queue as much as you like. Jobs wait their turn, and same-model jobs are grouped for you. A swap between models costs load time. A batch of twenty concepts, then twenty meshes, loads each model once. Close games and video before a heavy step, or let the step wait. A take made at a lighter profile than you asked for says so. Retake it when the card is free. If you point Gen Studio at your own ComfyUI or llama.cpp server in ~/.config/gen-studio/config.toml, it uses it and never stops it. Its VRAM is yours to manage.
Use the queue Batches overnight Profiles and target looks Troubleshooting

Why does Gen Studio run every model on your own machine, and what does that cost you? Gen Studio doesn't call an online service to make anything. The network is used for what you ask for: downloading models and runtimes, searching free asset libraries, and the phone page, which stays on your local network behind a token.

Every picture and sound in these docs comes from one sample project: about forty assets, from anime shots to a rigged character, a music loop and item text. Two batch files made them on one RTX 4090. Nothing was uploaded to make them, and no credits were counted. Each take's meta.json pins the model revision, the workflow and the seed, so the same files can be made again long after.

Your work stays yours. Prompts, reference pictures, imported models and results stay on your disk. That matters for an unreleased game or work under NDA. The same result, later. An online service changes its models without telling you. Here every model is pinned to an exact revision and every workflow to its hash. gen update writes the pins to gen.lock, and gen restore installs exactly them on another machine. No cost per take. Once the models are downloaded, a take costs electricity. Make twenty concepts to find one, or run a batch overnight. Nobody else's queue or terms. Nothing waits behind other people's jobs, and nothing stops working when a service shuts down. Standalone. Gen Studio installs and manages what it needs under one data folder: ComfyUI at a pinned commit, a llama.cpp server for text, one environment per model worker, and the model files. Licences on record. Local models come with a range of licences, some non-commercial. The licence of the model behind every take, and the source and licence of every free asset you import, are written in the take. Gen Studio doesn't decide for you, but you can see what your game is built from before you ship it.

You need a capable GPU. Gen Studio is built and tested on an RTX 4090 with 24 GB. Several steps want 16 to 24 GB of VRAM. A smaller card limits what runs at Quality. You need disk space. The Minimal install is 80 GB, Recommended 266 GB, Full 358 GB. Models can go on another drive. The first install takes a while. Downloads resume and are checked by hash. A hosted model may be faster per picture. Fast profiles keep trying-out short; Quality is for the keepers. One heavy model runs at a time. Jobs queue, and the scheduler swaps models for you.

The words Gen Studio uses, in alphabetical order. New here? Read the window in five minutes first.
A cut-out drawing split into parts on Godot bones (Skeleton2D), with idle, sway and head-tilt animations.
An extension that adds another model to its parent extension's steps, and is on only while the parent is on.
One thing you make, such as a prop, a character, a sound or a texture, kept as a folder in the project's assets folder.
What sort of asset it is (prop, character, music, anime shot), which decides the steps it starts with.
A project setting that makes a finished step start the next one by itself, up to the next review.
One measure of a composed piece; the composer's editor locks, rerolls and rewrites a piece bar by bar.
A plain body (underwear, a bodysuit, a mannequin) that a wardrobe of pieces fits onto.
A file of many jobs, with optional prompt, seed and profile combinations, that runs at low priority, for example overnight.
Another word for a path: a second route from a step, kept beside the first.
An animation on a character's rig, made from text or from a video, with its own row on the step rail.
Bone chains down what hangs (a cape, a skirt, long hair) that Godot's spring-bone simulator swings while the game runs.
The first picture of a prop or character, drawn so a 3D model can be built from it.
A picture with its background removed, so only the subject is left.
A pack of steps, models and asset kinds described by a gen-extension.toml file, which you turn on or off in Settings.
The name the CLI and the project files use for the target look.
The 3D model rebuilt within your target look's triangle budget, with its texture baked; the step's id is retopo.
The dense 3D model of a character, built from its turnaround and used only to make the game mesh.
A new try at the picked bars of a composed piece, made with New idea and listed as a take to compare.
The one take of a step that the next steps are built from.
An optional recipe for a step: a model, its limits, sometimes a LoRA, and passes that run after it.
A folder on any drive where model files and their environments live.
A small file added to an image model that teaches it one character or one style.
The Model Context Protocol, which lets an agent such as Claude Code drive Gen Studio through the gen-mcp server.
The dense 3D model of a prop, built from its concept and used only to make the game mesh.
On a step that more than one model can run, the field that picks which one runs it.
A named set of a base body's wardrobe pieces.
A set of steps and their models that you turn on or off together; the same thing as an extension.
A row of steps on an asset; a path started from a step of another row is named b1, b2 and so on.
The steps an asset kind starts with, in order, such as a prop's Concept, Prepped cut-out, Mesh and Game mesh.
How long a step may take (Ultra fast, Fast, Balanced or Quality), which picks the model and its settings.
The record in every take's meta.json of exactly how it was made, so it can be made again.
The list of jobs waiting for the GPU, where one big model runs at a time.
A new seed that replaces a take; the old take goes to the project's .trash folder.
A new take of a step, kept beside the others until you choose to use it.
A stop after a step where you check the result before the rest runs; Continue runs on.
A model with a skeleton and skin weights, its bones named for Godot's humanoid profile; the step's id is skin.
Several variants of one sound effect, so repeats don't sound the same.
The number that fixes a model's random choices, so the same seed with the same settings gives the same result.
Where a wardrobe piece goes (feet, outer torso) and how far out it sits, from 0 skin-tight to 3 outer.
A shot of an anime character in every expression, with talking and blinking frames.
A step built from a take that's no longer in use: still there, but out of date until it runs again.
One part of a track split out by the Stems step, such as the drums, the bass or the vocals.
One stage of making an asset, with its own form and its own takes.
One try at a step: Take 3 in the app, v003 in folders and on the CLI.
The era your game looks like, PS1 to PS4, which sets triangle and texture budgets and clip frame rates.
How much the install downloads: Minimal, Recommended or Full.
A character drawn from the front, left, back and right, for building it in 3D.
The graphics card's memory, which most steps want most of.
A piece of clothing or armour made for one rigged character or base body and skinned to its skeleton.
A model's files, pinned by exact revision and hash and downloaded on install or on first use.
A model's own process and Python environment, started when a step needs it.
A small text model on your CPU behind the sparkle and dice buttons of a prompt field.
