Everything the app does, and more, from a terminal. Run it from a project folder, or pass --project. Each command's help is below, as gen --help prints it.

What each target look (fidelity in files and on the CLI) sets by default. A project can override the budgets in gen-project.toml ([budgets.prop], [budgets.character]); a take can set its own triangles and texture on the Game mesh step.
The files you can write by hand: a project, a job, an extension's manifest.
What Export copies into res://assets/gen/, and their functions.
What kind: in a job file makes, and the steps it runs, by their ids. In the app these are in New asset; the wiki has a page for each.
What Claude Code (or another MCP client) can call on gen-mcp --project .
Every pinned weights file, by extension and group (gen install weights --group ), with its exact revision and licence. Licences are recorded in each take that uses them.
The app's keys. Help → Keyboard shortcuts shows them too. Text fields keep their own keys.
Every step a pipeline can run by its id, the model each profile uses, and its form. The keys go after --set on the CLI. The wiki has the same steps with tips.

Everything the app does, and more, from a terminal. Run it from a project folder, or pass --project. Each command's help is below, as gen <command> --help prints it. usage: gen [-h] [--version] {setup,doctor,run,make,mcp,serve,dock,batch,import,find,status,outfit,promote,retake,reroll,run-to,add-step,branch,rerun-stale,discard,delete-step,clone,export,install,ext,kit,config,library,data,queue,new,update,restore} ... Gen Studio positional arguments: {setup,doctor,run,make,mcp,serve,dock,batch,import,find,status,outfit,promote,retake,reroll,run-to,add-step,branch,rerun-stale,discard,delete-step,clone,export,install,ext,kit,config,library,data,queue,new,update,restore} setup set up Gen Studio: folder, tier, packs, imports, then install doctor check Python, uv, GPU, driver, disk and ComfyUI run run a job file through the slice, or check a meta.json make quick job without a file, e.g. gen make prop "an oak barrel" mcp Claude Code: add the MCP server and the gen-studio skill serve the queue on your phone (LAN page with a token) dock the Gen Studio dock in a Godot project (talks to gen serve) batch queue many jobs from one file (jobs and a matrix) import bring in a model you have (fbx, obj, glb, vrm, blend) find search free models, textures, sounds, music, shaders and voices status an asset's step versions, canonical ones and stale steps outfit save a base body's named set of wardrobe pieces promote make a candidate version of a step canonical retake one more take of a step (kept until you promote it) reroll a new seed for a take, replacing it (the old one's pictures kept in rerolls/) run-to build or refresh an asset's steps up to this one add-step add a step after the last one of a path branch start a new path from any step (b<n>/<stage>) rerun-stale refresh every stale step of an asset, clips too discard move a take that isn't in use to the project's .trash delete-step move a step, the steps after it and paths from them to .trash clone copy a whole asset (its takes and picks) to a new id export copy an asset's finished result into a Godot project install install a managed runtime or model weights ext list or validate extensions kit Kits: optional recipes for a step config settings kept outside config.toml library library folders: where models and envs live data the data folder: move it, see what uses the space, import queue work through queued jobs new scaffold a new extension update write gen.lock from the installed extensions and runtimes restore install and verify exactly what gen.lock pins options: -h, --help show this help message and exit --version show program's version number and exit

usage: gen add-step [-h] [--project PROJECT] asset after stage positional arguments: asset after the step it follows: the end of the main path or of a b<n> path stage what it runs, e.g. image_to_mesh (gen ext list shows stages) options: -h, --help show this help message and exit --project PROJECT
usage: gen batch [-h] batch_file positional arguments: batch_file options: -h, --help show this help message and exit

usage: gen branch [-h] [--project PROJECT] asset step stage positional arguments: asset step the step the new path starts from stage the new path's first step, e.g. reframe options: -h, --help show this help message and exit --project PROJECT

usage: gen clone [-h] [--as NEW_ID] [--project PROJECT] asset positional arguments: asset options: -h, --help show this help message and exit --as NEW_ID the copy's id (default: <asset>_copy, _copy_2, ...) --project PROJECT
usage: gen config [-h] {civitai-key} ... positional arguments: {civitai-key} civitai-key the Civitai API key (read from a prompt or stdin) options: -h, --help show this help message and exit

usage: gen data [-h] {move,usage,import} ... positional arguments: {move,usage,import} move copy the data folder to <path>, verify, then symlink usage space used by weights, projects, caches, envs, orphans import bring model files you already have, matched by sha256 options: -h, --help show this help message and exit
usage: gen delete-step [-h] [--yes] [--project PROJECT] asset step positional arguments: asset step options: -h, --help show this help message and exit --yes don't ask --project PROJECT

usage: gen discard [-h] [--yes] [--project PROJECT] asset step version positional arguments: asset step version e.g. 2 or v002 options: -h, --help show this help message and exit --yes don't ask --project PROJECT
usage: gen dock [-h] {install} ... positional arguments: {install} install copy the dock add-on into a Godot project and enable it options: -h, --help show this help message and exit

usage: gen doctor [-h] [--reindex [PROJECT]] [--relink] [--verify] options: -h, --help show this help message and exit --reindex [PROJECT] rebuild gen.db from a project's asset folders (default: current project) --relink rebuild the view's links from the online libraries --verify --relink: match by sha256, not size

usage: gen export [-h] [--step STEP] [--project PROJECT] asset godot positional arguments: asset godot the Godot project folder (has project.godot) options: -h, --help show this help message and exit --step STEP export this step's take, e.g. the end of a path: b1/retouch --project PROJECT

usage: gen ext [-h] {list,enable,disable,move,validate} ... positional arguments: {list,enable,disable,move,validate} list installed extensions (on or off) and their stages enable turn an extension on disable turn an extension off move move an extension to another library (resumable) validate check manifests, pins, envs and quality.toml options: -h, --help show this help message and exit

usage: gen find [-h] [--textures] [--sounds] [--music] [--shaders] [--voices] query positional arguments: query options: -h, --help show this help message and exit --textures --sounds --music --shaders --voices

What Export copies into res://assets/gen/, and their functions.

Gen Studio wardrobe (spec 016): dress a base body at runtime. Each piece's .glb has a .wardrobe.json beside it (its slot, layer, the body vertices it covers and its cloth chains); outfits.json beside the body names sets of pieces. Wardrobe.equip($Body, "res://assets/gen/coat/coat.glb") Wardrobe.unequip($Body, "torso_outer") Wardrobe.wear_outfit($Body, "res://assets/gen/hero/outfits.json", "travel") One piece per slot is worn; putting one on takes off what was in its slot. The body under what's worn is hidden (its triangles left out), so it can't poke through. static func worn(character: Node) -> Dictionary: What a character wears: slot -> {"path", "info"} (kept on the character as meta). static func equip(character: Node, piece_path: String) -> void static func unequip(character: Node, slot: String) -> void static func wear_outfit(character: Node, outfits_path: String, outfit: String) -> void

Gen Studio wearables (spec 011): put a piece on a character at runtime. The piece's .glb shares the character's skeleton (same bone names and rest pose), so its meshes move onto the character's Skeleton3D and follow every animation. Wearables.wear($Knight, preload("res://assets/gen/leather_boots/leather_boots.glb")) Wearables.remove($Knight, "leather_boots") A piece with cloth chains (spec 014: a cape, a skirt) brings its extra bones, and the .cloth.json beside it sets up a SpringBoneSimulator3D on the skeleton: one setting per chain, its material's stiffness, drag and gravity, capsule colliders on the body. A character's own chains (its long hair) come from its .cloth.json the same way: Wearables.cloth($Girl, "res://assets/gen/girl/girl.cloth.json") (the exported _cloth.tscn already does this). static func wear(character: Node, piece: PackedScene) -> Array[MeshInstance3D]: Instance piece and move its meshes onto character's skeleton; returns them. static func cloth(character: Node, path: String) -> void: Set up the simulator for a character's own chains (its hair) from its .cloth.json. static func remove(character: Node, piece_name: String) -> void: Take off a piece put on with wear() (by its scene's name).

A Gen Studio sprite or portrait set: put this on an AnimatedSprite2D whose sprite_frames is the set's sprite_frames.tres. Each expression is an animation; "_talk" flaps the mouth and "_blink" closes the eyes, which happens by itself every few seconds. func show_expression(name: String) -> void func talk(on: bool) -> void

Gen Studio toon look: on load, every MeshInstance3D under this node gets toon.gdshader with its own albedo (texture and colour) and outline.gdshader as the next pass. Rigs and clips keep animating (only materials change). func apply(node: Node) -> void

What Claude Code (or another MCP client) can call on gen-mcp --project <game>.

Add a step that runs stage after the step after (see next_steps); returns its key. branch starts a new path there (b/): the main path stays as it is, use it for an edit you may not keep or when after already has a next step. Adding in line a stage the template doesn't have takes the template's remaining steps off the path, so it's refused unless you pass branch or inline. To run it: fields, then retake. Arguments: name, after, stage, branch, inline
Give another character the same motion: clip of source becomes the clip name of target, retargeted onto its rig. Arguments: source, clip, target, name

An asset's graph: steps lists every step, also those not run yet, with its key (what you pass to other tools; stage is what runs: the key skin runs the stage rig), state (done, stale, queued, running, failed, not started), after, takes and the take in use. A gate step waits for your review; run_to carries on. b/... are paths from a step, clips//... a character's clips. Arguments: name
Cancel a job: a queued one at once, a running one at its next check (and the steps queued after it). Arguments: job_id

Godot 4.7's import checks on the takes in use (or one step's): a game mesh imports, a rig has its bones and skinned meshes, a clip its length, loop and drift, a shader compiles; plus what the steps measured (turnaround sides, wearable view agreement, the body poking through a piece). Problems are listed; an empty list means all is well. Arguments: name, step
Takes of a step side by side in one labelled image (default: all, at most 6), each shown by its first picture; the text lists them as look does. Arguments: name, step, versions

Take a step away, with the steps after it on its row and the paths from them: to the project's .trash, never deleted outright. Without confirm it only reports what would go; tell the user before you confirm. Arguments: name, step, confirm
Move a take that isn't in use to the project's .trash. Without confirm it only says what it would do. Arguments: name, step, version, confirm

Copy an asset's finished result into a Godot project (assets/gen//). It reads the last step on the main path that makes the asset's kind of result, a step you added included; step names another, e.g. the end of a path (b1/retouch). The reply says which it read. Arguments: name, godot_project, step

A step's form, whether it has run or not: each field (label, type, default, choices, descriptions, help) with its value in use, the profiles and models it can run with and what each would download, and also: arguments outside the form. retake takes all of them. stage alone gives a stage's form before you add it (from next_steps). Arguments: name, step, stage

Search free assets online: kind is model, texture, sound, music, shader or voice. Each result has its uri, licence and page; bring one in with make(kind="import_prop" (or import_character, import_texture, import_sfx, import_music, import_shader, import_voice), asset, fields={"model" for models, else "source": uri, "licence": ...}). Arguments: query, kind

How a stage works: page is its wiki page (what it does, what it runs, how long, its fields); models its prompt guide where it has one (summary, structure, tips, what to avoid and examples, per model and profile). next_steps and asset give the stage ids. Arguments: stage

Download weights groups (the group of a refusal's needs) as a queue row beside the GPU job, to where the user's libraries place them. Ask the user first and say the size: without confirm this only reports the size. Arguments: groups, confirm
A job's status (queued, running, done, failed, cancelled), phase, progress and error; when done, its result files. Arguments: job_id
The queue, every project's since the GPU is shared: active (running and queued, with asset, step, phase and progress) and failed (recent failures with their errors). Arguments: limit

What can be made: each kind's steps (key is what you pass, stage what runs; gate stops a chain for review, manual you start yourself), its first form, extras a job can take beyond it. Advanced fields are by name: fields(stage=...) has them whole. off: packs that are off, and the command for the user to run. Arguments: none

See a take (default: the one in use): pictures as images with their sizes, a model as a labelled sheet of four views, a clip or video as frames, a sound as a waveform, text inline. grid draws a labelled 10 % grid on each, for reading positions for make_mask and select_part (as fractions, x then y, from the top left). Arguments: name, step, version, grid

Queue a new asset of kind (see kinds) named asset (lowercase, a-z0-9_-) with its form fields, e.g. {"prompt": "an oak barrel", "profile": "fast"}; extras in kinds go there too (a clip's clip). A model that isn't installed is refused with its size unless on_missing is "install" (ask the user first) or "fast". Returns the queued job ids. Arguments: kind, asset, fields, on_missing

Draw a mask for Retouch's mask or Erase's erase, at the picture's exact size. step is the Retouch step (it draws on the picture before it) or the Rim light, Relight or other step whose take you mean (version, default in use). shapes is a list of {box: [left, top, right, bottom]} or {polygon: [[x, y], ...]}, as fractions of the picture; look with grid=true helps you read them. soft feathers the edge, in pixels. Returns the path to pass as the field and a picture of the area in red: check it before you run. Naming the area with Retouch's find is usually better than drawing it. Arguments: name, step, shapes, version, invert, soft

What can follow a step (the app's Add step, Branch from here): fits lists each stage with what it does, its group, seconds, the model at the project's profile, the download it needs, and recommended for the template's next; not_now lists those that can't, and why. Then fields(stage=...), add_step, and retake to run it. Arguments: name, step
Save a base body's named set of wardrobe pieces (wearable assets made for it); export writes it to outfits.json. Arguments: body, name, pieces
Which round-robin variants of a sound take go on to Clean up and Effects (an empty list: all of them). The steps after it go stale. Arguments: name, step, version, names
The project: its target look (ps1 to ps4), default profile, triangle and texture budgets, audio format, and each asset with its kind and the last step that has a take. Arguments: none
A new seed for a take (default: the one in use), the same settings, replacing it when done; its old pictures stay in rerolls/, the old take goes to .trash. Arguments: name, step, version
Refresh every stale step of an asset, its clips too. Arguments: name

Run a step with these values: another take, or a step's first (a new step's first take is used by itself; later ones wait for use). Takes any field of fields(name, step) plus its also arguments; unset ones keep their last values (the reply shows them; null clears one). on_missing as for make. Arguments: name, step, fields, on_missing

Your verdict on a take waiting for review (job says needs_review; with [agent] judge = "agent" the local model doesn't judge): accept it or not, with notes. It goes into the take's judge.json and notes; use it, or submit a fix as a new take. Arguments: name, step, accept, notes, version

Queue an asset's missing or stale steps up to step (a key from asset), as one chain (the app's Run to end); with only_stale, refresh stale steps without building missing ones. on_missing as for make. Arguments: name, step, only_stale, on_missing

Mark a part of a mesh or rig take for Edit part's selection, as the viewer's Select part does. Each click is {view: "front"|"left"|"back"|"right", x, y, sign}: x and y are fractions within that panel of look's four-view sheet (grid=true helps), sign 1 for the part, -1 for what isn't. With brush (a share of the model's size, e.g. 0.05) each click marks the faces around it directly; without it the job's SAM 3.1 grows a click into the part. Blender on the CPU, a few seconds. Returns the path to pass as selection and the views with what the clicks hit tinted. Naming the part with region is usually better than clicking. Arguments: name, step, clicks, version, brush

The machine, read-only: packs on and off, weights by install tier with sizes, library folders with free space, first-run setup, and the doctor's failures. Agents don't change these: for_the_user_to_run names the commands to pass on. Arguments: none

Hand in a file you made (a fixed .gdshader, an edited PNG, a .glb), or a result from a path (a retouched picture back to its concept), as a new take of a step: it replaces one output (output, default the first) of take version (default the one in use), the rest is copied, and the take records "agent: claude-code". It isn't used until you use it. A Retouch mask isn't a take: make_mask writes it, the step's mask field reads it. Arguments: name, step, file, output, version, note
A step's takes, oldest first: version, in use, seed, profile, prompt, the form values asked for, rating and favourite, and its files. Arguments: name, step
Make take version of a step the one in use (later steps then show as stale). Arguments: name, step, version
Block until a job ends (done, failed, cancelled) or timeout_s passes, then report it as job does; call it again while the status is still queued or running. Arguments: job_id, timeout_s

Every pinned weights file, by extension and group (gen install weights --group <group>), with its exact revision and licence. Licences are recorded in each take that uses them. Tier (spec 027): gen install weights installs Minimal and Recommended (--tier minimal only the first, --tier full On demand too). An On demand model downloads the first time a step needs it, after the app asks; By name ones only with --group. Tiers are worked out from the recipes, with every pack's default settings (the anime pack's groups count when it is on). The app's keys. Help → Keyboard shortcuts shows them too. Text fields keep their own keys.

Keys What it does Ctrl+K Command palette: actions, this asset's steps, assets Ctrl+N New asset Ctrl+1 Home Ctrl+2 Assets Ctrl+W Close the asset tab Ctrl+, Settings F1 Help, on the step you're on F5 Refresh Assets Ctrl+Q Quit
Keys What it does [ and ] Previous and next step ← and → Previous and next take R A new take U Use the picked take Ctrl+Enter Generate, in a form

Keys What it does 1 to 8 View modes: shaded, base colour, wireframe, normals, roughness, metalness, UV checker, PS1 G Floor grid H A 1.8 m figure for scale F Frame the model R Reset the view B Bones Drag Orbit Right- or middle-drag Pan Wheel Zoom [ and ] Brush size, in Select part

Keys What it does B Brush E Eraser L Lasso R Box K Click (SAM) [ and ] Brush size (also Ctrl + wheel) M Show the area Hold \ The picture without the area Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Shift+Z Undo, redo F Fit 1 100 % Space-drag, middle-drag Pan
Keys What it does Space Play and pause ← and → Seek (Shift: further) Home, End To the start, to the end L Loop
Drag up and down (Shift: finer). The wheel and ↑ / ↓ step it. Double-click for the default.
Every step a pipeline can run by its id, the model each profile uses, and its form. The keys go after --set on the CLI. The wiki has the same steps with tips.

Light from light choice (upper_right, upper_left, right, left, top, bottom) upper_right Which side the rim light comes from. Strength strength int 1.0…5.0 3 1 a faint line to 5 wide, bright bands. The result changes with the seed: make another take (or Reroll) until one lands. Keep only the rim colour filter bool False Drops whatever the relight painted that isn't the rim colour (a sleeve or armband it invented). The unfiltered take is kept too. Third character's outfit character3_outfit text A named outfit from the third character's Outfits. (advanced) Fourth character character4 asset A fourth Anime character (optional). (advanced) Fourth character's outfit character4_outfit text A named outfit from the fourth character's Outfits. (advanced) Layout layout file Where each character stands, for two or more: empty for equal columns, or a rough drawing with one filled box per character in red, green, blue, yellow (in their order). (advanced)

How it moves motion longtext What happens over time: 'bursts outward, then the flames curl up and fade to smoke' Loop loop bool False For fire, auras and steady effects: the last frames blend into the first Length (seconds) duration float 1.0…5.0 2 How long the effect lasts, up to 5 s (what the video model draws in one pass). One piece at a time. Character character text The character asset (it needs its Rig step). Slot slot choice (auto, head, hair, face, neck, torso_inner, torso_outer, hands, waist, legs, feet, back, accessory) auto Where it goes in the character's wardrobe: one piece per slot and layer is worn at a time. Layer layer choice (auto, 0, 1, 2, 3) auto A piece is fitted over the same character's pieces on lower layers: a coat (2) over a shirt (1). (advanced) Cloth cloth choice (auto, none, cape, skirt, hair, tail) auto Bone chains down the parts that hang, so they swing in Godot. Built into the core (no model). Field Type Default What it does Route route choice (auto, conforming, rigid, sheet) auto Follows the body: boots, gloves, shirts, trousers are made from the body's own surface, so they fit by construction. Rigid: helmets, pauldrons, belts are built in 3D from the four views, then fitted. Hanging sheet: a cape, its outline from the back view, hung behind the body. Auto picks a sheet for a cape, else by how far the piece stands off the body. Thickness thickness float 0.0…0.05 0.0 How thick a piece that follows the body is, in metres (0: 0.6 % of the character's height) (advanced)
Every part of the main window and what it's for, in the order you meet them. Read this once, then make something in First launch.

An asset is one thing you make: a prop, a character, a sound. A step is one stage of making it: Concept, Mesh, Game mesh. A take is one try at a step. Takes stay until you discard them. The take in use is the one the next step builds from. Use a different take, and the steps built from the old one turn stale: still there, but out of date. More in steps and paths.

The top bar has the menus (File, Edit, View, Help), then Home and Assets, then one tab per open asset. At its right end are the project's name and Settings. The status bar along the bottom shows the running job, then CPU, RAM, GPU and VRAM, and Queue.

The app opens here. It answers two questions: what's happening, and what needs you? The prompt bar makes something straight away. Pick a kind, write a line, pick a profile and press Make it. All kinds… opens the full list. You can also drop a picture, a model or a sound on it to import that file. Latest takes shows the newest result of each asset. Click one to open it. Right-click for Open, Clone and Delete…. Waiting for you lists what can't go on without you: failures, reviews, stale steps. Each card has its fix. With nothing waiting it says "All clear". On the GPU shows the running job, what's Up next and what's holding the VRAM. Projects switches between your games. A project is a folder with a gen-project.toml in it. New project… asks for a folder and a Target look; Open folder… opens one you have.

Every asset in the project. Press Assets in the top bar, or Ctrl+2. It's greyed out until a project is open. The left side filters. All assets, then your groups, then Smart filters: Needs you, Working, Stale, Favourites and Not exported. The cards are one per asset. The bar under each card has one segment per step, in the step's status colour. Click a card to see its steps on the right. Double-click to open it. Right-click a card to open it, mark it a favourite, Re-run stale, Export to Godot, Show in folder, Clone or Delete…. The top row has the search, the sort (Last changed, Name, Kind), the card size, Find free assets and New asset.

Ctrl+N, All kinds… on Home, or New asset on Assets. Start from picks between From a description and From a file. The middle lists the kinds, each with a picture of what it makes; the search finds one by name. The right side shows Its steps, so you see the route before you start, then the Asset name, the Profile, the Seed and the kind's own fields. Generate queues the first step.
This is where the work happens. Each open asset is a tab in the top bar.

The asset's name, then what you do to the whole asset: Export to Godot, Auto-continue, Run to end and the ⋮ menu. Re-run stale shows only when something is stale. Continue shows when a step waits for your review. ⋮ has New clip and Wardrobe on a character, Clone asset and Delete asset…. Deleting moves the asset to the project's .trash folder.

The asset's steps, left to right, as pills. A dot on each shows its status. Click one to open it. The dashed + at the end of a row opens Add step: what can follow, with the model each runs and about how long it takes. Right-click a pill for Retake, Run to here, Branch from here…, Cancel its runs, Show in folder and Delete step…. A branch is a second row, named b1, b2. A character's clips have rows of their own. An asset made from another one (a shot from its character) starts with that asset's pill, marked source. It's there to look at. See add steps and paths.
On the left: what the step builds from, then its form. Profile first, then the prompt and the step's own fields. Advanced shows the rest, and Presets. The fields are the ones in the steps reference.

The picked take, large, in the middle. A picture, a 3D view you can turn, a waveform or text, depending on the step. Double-click it, or press Open large, for the big viewer. The bar above it has the take's tools and one green button: New take or Retake, or Use and run with the next step's name, which uses the picked take and runs the step after it. Its ⋯ menu has Run next. The strip below holds every take of this step, oldest first, ending with the New take card. The take in use is marked. Right-click a take for Use this take, Reroll (replace this take), a rating, compare and Discard…. A new take doesn't replace the one in use. You look, then choose. See retake and compare.

Details shows the facts of the file on the stage: the model, the seed, the time it took and the licence. On steps that change something you already have (Retouch, Edit part), the right side is a tool panel instead, and Details folds up at its foot.
The step shows a panel that says what went wrong in plain words and what to do. Copy log copies the job's log. The common ones are in troubleshooting.

Everything you start goes in the queue. One big model fits on the GPU at a time, so jobs wait their turn. Press Queue in the status bar. Each row is a job and links to its step. Pause lets the running job finish and starts nothing new; Resume carries on. Downloads have their own lane beside the GPU job. See use the queue and the VRAM scheduler.

Settings in the top bar, or Ctrl+,. Models: what's installed and what fits your GPU. Install and remove here. Project: this game's Target look (PS1 to PS4), Default profile, Auto-continue, and the sound format for export. Storage: your libraries, the data folder, what uses the space, and Clean up for old takes. Extensions: packs of steps and models, on and off. A change applies when you restart the app. Downloads: your Civitai API key, for models whose creator asks for a login. Appearance: theme, colours, text size and Reduce motion. Setup: Open setup shows the first-run window again. About: the version, the machine checks and licences. Two of these shape every result. Target look is the era your game looks like and sets the budgets. Profile is how long a step may take and picks the model. See profiles and target looks.

Help → Help…, or F1. On a step, F1 opens that step's page. The list has the step you're on, the asset kinds, the steps, the concepts, and troubleshooting and the glossary. What's new and Keyboard shortcuts are there too. Full guide on the website opens the same page here, with its pictures and clips. The Help menu also has Check this machine, which opens the checks in Settings → About.
Ctrl+K searches every action and asset. On an asset, [ and ] move between steps, ← and → between takes, R makes a new take and U uses the picked take. All of them: keyboard shortcuts.
First launch, then your first prop.
Find what you see, read why, then try the fixes in order. A failed step's panel says what went wrong and has Copy log. gen doctor checks the GPU, the driver, disk space and the runtimes.

Why: the top bar says "No project open" and Assets is greyed out until a project folder is open. On Home, press New project…, pick a folder and a Target look. Or press Open folder… and pick a folder that has a gen-project.toml in it.

Why: the model didn't fit beside what else uses the GPU: a game, a browser playing video, another AI tool. The message names the numbers: "needs about 21 GB of VRAM but only 9.5 GB is free". Look at Home's On the GPU to see what holds the memory, and close it. Gen Studio never stops a program it didn't start. Press Retake. If it still fails, pick a lighter Profile and retake. A step that runs out of memory part-way goes again one profile lighter by itself. Its queue row then says "Fell back: ran at Fast", and the take records it.
documents.s: A step failed with "Ran out of GPU memory"

documents.t: Why: that step's model hasn't been downloaded. The Recommended install leaves out models that only Balanced, Quality or a second Model choice use. In the app, press Download and run in the box that asks. It queues the download, then the step. Or press Run at Fast to run now with a model you have. In a terminal, run the command the message ends with: gen install weights --group <group>. To fetch every on-demand model at once: gen install weights --tier full (357.6 GB in all). The CLI, batches and agents don't ask. They refuse with the install command. The groups are in the models reference.
documents.s: A step says a model is "not installed"

documents.t: Why: a tool or runtime the step needs is missing. The message says which. "not installed (gen install workers)": run gen install workers from the Gen Studio folder. "llama.cpp isn't installed": run gen install llama.cpp. "ComfyUI: not installed" in gen doctor: run gen install comfyui. "the writing helper isn't installed": install the Text tools models in Settings → Models. "Blender is not on PATH" or "ffmpeg isn't installed": install it with your system's package manager. Or press Settings → Setup → Open setup and let Install queue what's missing.

Why: the pack that has it is off. The anime pack (gen.anime) and the pixel art and chiptune pack (gen.pixel) ship off. Open Settings → Extensions and switch the pack on. Or run gen ext enable gen.anime. Restart the app. A change applies on the next start. Install its models in Settings → Models, or let them download the first time a step asks. A Kit says "Kits need the … extension on" for the same reason. See extensions on and off.
documents.s: A kind or a step doesn't show, or "no installed extension provides the … stage"

documents.t: Why: a step was built from a take you no longer use, and export won't send Godot a half-updated asset. Open the asset and press Re-run stale. Or use the old take again, and nothing is stale. Export again. A take marked rebuild by hand was built on another take. See run the stale steps.

Why: steps that check their result in Godot, and export, need Godot 4.7 and a real project folder. Install Godot 4.7 so that godot runs in a terminal. "need Godot 4.7.x, found …" means another version is first on your PATH. For export, pick the folder that holds project.godot.
documents.s: "Godot 4.7 not found on PATH", or "is not a Godot project"

documents.t: Why: the model is in a library on a drive that isn't mounted. Connect the drive. The app checks every 10 seconds. Open Queue, hover the failed row and press Retry. If the drive mounts somewhere else now, see libraries and drives, or run gen doctor --relink.
documents.s: A step says a drive "isn't connected"

documents.t: Why: the model's worker didn't come up in time, or it exited. Press Retake once the GPU is free. A crashed worker is restarted once by itself. If it happens again, press Copy log and read the last lines. Run gen doctor. "Gen Studio hit a bug" or "The extension answered unexpectedly" is not something you did. Please report it with the log.
documents.s: "The model took too long to start" or "The model's process crashed"

documents.t: Why: you tried to delete a step while it, or a step after it, has a job. Open Queue and cancel the job, or right-click the step → Cancel its runs. Try again.
documents.s: "… is running or queued; cancel it first"

documents.t: Why: some Civitai files need an account, and some models on Hugging Face are gated behind a licence you accept on their page. Civitai: paste your API key in Settings → Downloads. A gated model: accept its licence on its Hugging Face page, then install it by name, for example gen install weights --group sonicmaster.
documents.s: A download asks for a login

documents.t: Too dark or flat: the export uses the baked texture. At PS1 and PS2 it's palette-reduced on purpose. Too many or too few polygons: the budget comes from the target look. Set the Game mesh step's Triangle budget. Parts are missing (a cart's wheel spokes, a lantern's ring handle): thin parts go first. Retake Mesh at Balanced or Quality, or make the concept simpler.
documents.s: The model looks wrong in Godot

documents.t: Why: the 3D model needs four fixed views, and the Turnaround got one wrong. It warns when it can't tell. Retake Turnaround. Run on from it.
documents.s: A character's left and right are swapped

documents.t: Why: the piece sits too close, or the piece under it wasn't there when it was fitted. Raise Clearance (metres) and retake. For a piece worn over another, make the lower Layer first. wear.json in the take lists the poke per test pose.
documents.s: A wearable pokes through the body

documents.t: Why: the piece's words didn't name something that hangs, or the swing settings don't suit it. Doesn't move: set Cloth to cape, skirt, hair or tail. Too floppy, too stiff, or "the cape chains stretch 8% in Godot": change Cloth material. A take fails above 5 % stretch. See cloth presets.
documents.s: Cloth doesn't move, or the take fails with "chains stretch"

documents.t: Run gen doctor. Press Copy log on the failed step and read the last lines. If the app's lists look wrong after you moved folders by hand, run gen doctor --reindex. It rebuilds the index from the asset folders.
Learn by doing. The path goes from first launch to a small scene in Godot, about two hours in all; each part ends with something you made and takes 10 to 20 minutes.

1 First launchYou set Gen Studio up, learn where things are in the window, and make one picture: the concept art of a market cart, with two takes to choose from. About 10 minutes, plus the downloads, which run in the background.2 Your first propYou make a brass lantern: concept art, a 3D model, a game mesh inside your target look's budget, and then the file in a Godot project. About 15 minutes, most of it waiting for the models.3 A character that movesYou make a courier for the village: concept, four views, a 3D model, a game mesh, a skeleton, and a walk clip that plays in Godot. About 20 minutes, most of it the model and rig steps.4 Textures, shaders and effectsYou make three things that aren't models: a cobblestone texture that tiles, with its maps and a Godot material; a pond-water shader that Godot compiles; and a blue flame as an animated flipbook. About 15 minutes.5 Sound and musicYou give the village its sound: two sound effects with variants, a looping theme, and a waltz written note by note that you can edit bar by bar. Then you clean one sound up and run it through effects. About 15 minutes.6 Voices and wordsYou design a voice for the village's potion seller, write a haggling scene as a dialogue file for Godot, write an item's text, and then have the scene spoken line by line. About 10 minutes.7 A small scene in GodotYou export everything from the earlier tutorials in one go, add the Gen Studio dock to the Godot editor, and build a small scene: the courier walking on a cobbled street beside a lantern, a pond, a blue flame, with the theme playing. About 15 minutes.8 Work fasterYou do what the earlier tutorials did without the window: one asset from a terminal, a file of jobs that runs overnight, and an agent that makes, looks and picks for you. About 15 minutes at the keyboard. The batch runs while you're away.

Once you know the window, in any order. An anime character with sprites and a 2D rigYou define an anime character once, take shots of her, then make a visual novel sprite set and a 2D rig for Godot. Noa, the alchemist on these pages, was made this way. About 30 minutes without her own LoRA. Training one adds 20 to 40 minutes. Pixel art and chiptuneYou turn on the pixel pack and make a small retro set: a potion sprite, a knight, a key icon, a sheet of meadow tiles, an overworld tune and a coin sound. The pictures are true pixels on a limited palette, not a big picture made to look blocky. About 15 minutes. A base body and an outfitYou make one plain body, dress it in pieces that fit over each other, save them as an outfit, and swap outfits at runtime in Godot. About 60 minutes for the body and four pieces. Most of that is the model and rig steps, which run without you. A clip from your phoneYou film yourself doing a move and put it on your character as a clip. About 5 minutes, plus the filming. A shader from a descriptionYou describe a shader in a sentence and get a .gdshader that compiles in Godot, with sliders for what you want to tweak. Then you read the judge's notes and steer a retake. About 5 minutes. Working with Claude Code over MCPYou connect Claude Code to a project and have it run Gen Studio for you: make assets, look at the takes, pick, retake and export. About 10 minutes.

You define an anime character once, take shots of her, then make a visual novel sprite set and a 2D rig for Godot. Noa, the alchemist on these pages, was made this way. About 30 minutes without her own LoRA. Training one adds 20 to 40 minutes. You'll make: a character sheet, the definition every shot copies shots of her: a transparent sprite and one in a scene a sprite set with expressions, for Ren'Py and Godot a 2D rig with three animations You'll learn: how one asset (a character) feeds others (shots, sets, rigs) framing, pose and background on a shot the rim light, and why you reroll it
documents.s: An anime character with sprites and a 2D rig

documents.t: Do first launch and your first prop. The anime pack is off by default. Turn it on in Settings → Extensions → gen.anime, restart the app, and install its models: gen ext enable gen.anime gen install weights --group anime

Press All kinds…, then Anime and Anime character. Describe her in Danbooru tags: who she is, hair, eyes, build and outfit. Noa's are: 1girl, solo, alchemist, short silver hair, bob cut, single long braid, teal eyes, small round earrings, dark navy long coat with brass buttons, rolled sleeves, cream knit sweater, leather belt with potion vials, brown shorts, black tights, short lace-up boots, brass goggles around neck Name the asset noa and press Generate. Checkpoint the Character sheet step shows her full body on white. Tags keep a character close, not exact. The optional Character LoRA step trains a small add-on for the drawing model on pictures of her. It takes 20 to 40 minutes and the whole GPU. Every shot of her uses it from then on.

Press All kinds…, then Anime and Shot of a character. Pick the Character. Set Framing to knee-up, the usual sprite, and Pose to standing. Set Background to Transparent for a sprite. Write the rest in Shot: gentle smile, looking at viewer, arms at sides Name it noa_up and press Generate. Make a second shot, noa_lanterns, with Background set to A scene: walking through a mountain village street at dusk, paper lanterns, festival stalls, looking back over shoulder, soft smile Checkpoint two Shot assets. Each rail starts with the character, marked source: her picture to look at, nothing to change there. Up to four characters fit in one shot. With three or more, each is redrawn in its own place (Layout), so they don't swap clothes.

The optional Rim light step paints a bright, thin rim on the edges facing a light, like fighting-game key art. Open a shot and press Add step at the end of the rail. Pick Rim light. Pick the Rim colour and Light from. Set how strong it is. The default model has Intensity, 1 to 5: 1 is a crisp, thin rim. With Model set to Qwen-Image-Edit 2511 the setting is Strength, and Keep only the rim colour drops anything else the relight painted. Press New take. Checkpoint the take shows the lit picture, with her edges on the light's side glowing. The result changes with the seed. If the rim is faint, right-click the take and press Reroll: a new seed that replaces the take. gen retake noa_up anime_rim --set intensity=2 gen reroll noa_up anime_rim

Press All kinds…, then Anime and Sprite or portrait set. Pick the knee-up Shot, noa_up. Write the Expressions you want: neutral, happy, angry, surprised, sad, smug. Name it noa_set and press Generate. Checkpoint one picture per expression, as at the top of this page. Each has talking and blinking frames. You also get a faceset, and files for Ren'Py (.rpy) and Godot (sprite_frames.tres with portrait.gd).

Press All kinds…, then Anime and 2D rig (cut-out animation). Pick the same transparent shot, name it noa_rig, and press Generate. Press Export to Godot and open noa_rig.tscn in Godot. Noa's 2D rig, idle Checkpoint the AnimationPlayer plays idle on start: she breathes, and her back hair swings. The shot is split into parts (hair, face, arms, legs, torso), the hidden areas are filled in, and you get a Godot scene with bones and three animations: idle breathing, a sway and a head tilt.
A character defined once, then shot in any framing. Her own LoRA for an exact look. The rim light, sprite sets and 2D rigs.
Pixel art and chiptune, or go back to the tutorials.
The anime kinds don't show: see troubleshooting. The rim is faint or lands in the wrong place: reroll the take. A hand or a face is off in a shot: retouch a picture.

You make a courier for the village: concept, four views, a 3D model, a game mesh, a skeleton, and a walk clip that plays in Godot. About 20 minutes, most of it the model and rig steps. You'll make: courier, a rigged character with bones named for Godot's humanoid profile a looping walk clip inside its .glb You'll learn: a character's steps: Concept, Turnaround, High poly, Game mesh, Rig what a review is, and how to check a rig before you go on clips, which sit on their own row of the rail
Do your first prop. This tutorial uses the same project, takes and export. The clip step at Fast, Balanced and Quality needs a motion model. If it isn't installed, the app asks before it downloads.

Press All kinds… on Home, then Characters & bodies and 3D game character. Write this in Prompt: a young courier with short auburn hair, goggles on her forehead, a short teal jacket over a cream shirt, brown trousers, sturdy boots, arms held away from the body Type courier in Asset name and press Generate. Make a second take with Retake if the first isn't right. Click the one you want. The concept is drawn in an A-pose with the arms away from the body, so it builds cleanly in 3D. Keep held things out of the prompt: a sword fused to a hand can't be rigged. Make it a prop. Checkpoint the Concept step shows the whole courier, head to boots, arms away from her sides, on a plain background.

With your concept take picked, press Use and run Turnaround. If the take is already in use, open the ⋯ menu in the same bar and press Run next: Turnaround. When it finishes, check the four pictures: front, left, back, right. Look for two things. Left and right aren't swapped: a detail on one side, like a pocket, stays on that side. And all four show the same character, with nothing added or dropped. If a view is wrong, press Retake. The step warns you when it can't tell left from right. Checkpoint four views of one courier, at fixed quarter turns. The 3D model is only as good as these.

Press Run to end. Three steps run: High poly builds the dense model from the four views. Game mesh fits it to your target look's budget. Rig adds the skeleton and the skin weights in one pass. Rig is a review: the run stops there for you to check. Click Rig, then Open large. Press Bones (or B) to see the skeleton inside the body. Turn the model and check the joints sit where they should: shoulders, elbows, hips, knees. When it looks right, close the viewer and press Continue in the toolbar. Check the rig before you make clips. If a joint is off, Edit joints in the viewer lets you move it, and the Rig step's Keep the skeleton (re-skin only) setting then redoes only the weights. Fixing a joint after you have clips means making the clips again. Checkpoint the rail reads Concept, Turnaround, High poly, Game mesh, Rig, all finished. Long hair or a cape? The Rig step's Cloth setting (Auto) adds bone chains down long hair, so it swings in Godot. See cloth presets. Capes and hats are wearables.

Press ⋮ in the toolbar, then New clip. Leave Make on A motion. Type walk in Clip name. Write this in Describe the motion: a person walks forward at a steady pace Leave Length at 3 seconds and press Generate. The clip gets its own row on the rail. When it's done, open it large and press play. the courier's walk clip One action per clip works best. A clip loops and stays in place by default: the end meets the start and the hips don't wander, so your game moves the character, not the animation. A job file can turn those off: # walk.yaml, run with: gen run walk.yaml asset: courier kind: motion clip: walk prompt: a person walks forward at a steady pace Add loop: false or in_place: false to change the defaults. Checkpoint the rail has a second row with the walk clip, and the courier walks on the spot in the viewer.

Press Export to Godot. In Godot, open res://assets/gen/courier/ and drag the .glb into a scene. Select its AnimationPlayer. The walk is in the list, and Godot loops clips whose names end in _loop. Checkpoint the courier walks in your Godot scene.

A character is a prop's idea with two more needs: four matching views, and a skeleton. A review stops the run until you press Continue. Clips are made after the rig, each on its own row, and travel inside the character's .glb.
Textures, shaders and effects: the street she walks on, the pond, and a blue flame. Or stay with characters: a clip from your phone, or a base body and an outfit.

Left and right are swapped: see troubleshooting. The clip slides, or the feet float: see troubleshooting. Hair doesn't move, or cloth explodes: see troubleshooting and cloth presets. "Needs a download": see troubleshooting.

You connect Claude Code to a project and have it run Gen Studio for you: make assets, look at the takes, pick, retake and export. About 10 minutes. You'll make: a prop, made, picked and exported by an agent You'll learn: how to install the MCP server and its skill which tools the agent uses, and what it sees what it leaves to you
documents.s: Working with Claude Code over MCP

documents.t: Claude Code installed. A project with a working setup: do your first prop first. Work faster introduces this in a few steps. This page has the detail.

Run this once: gen mcp install --project ~/gen/lantern-village It adds the gen-studio MCP server at user scope, and the gen-studio skill. Start a new Claude Code session. Ask what it can see: what's in my Gen Studio project? Checkpoint the agent lists your assets and their steps.

Ask for something with a choice in it: Make a wooden barrel. Show me two takes of the concept, use the better one and export it to ~/games/lantern-village. Watch it work. It starts the job, waits, and looks at the takes as pictures. Open the app beside it. The same asset is there with the same takes: the agent and the app share the project and the queue. Ask it to change something: the hoops should be iron, not rope. It retakes the step, or adds a Retouch or an Edit part step. Checkpoint the barrel is in the project and in Godot, and the agent said which take it used and what it saw. What it uses: make, wait, job: start and follow jobs; look, compare: see takes as pictures (four views of a model, frames of a clip, a sound's waveform); asset, next_steps, add_step, fields, retake, use, run_to: the step graph; make_mask, select_part: the area to retouch or the part to edit, when naming it isn't enough; check, export: Godot's import checks, then the export.

Ask it for something that needs a model you don't have. It asks you before a download. Ask it to delete a step. It can only move steps and takes to the project's .trash. Ask it to turn on an extension. It tells you the command: extensions and library folders are yours. Checkpoint in each case the agent stopped and asked, or handed you a command, and didn't act on its own.

gen mcp install --scope project --project ~/your-game gives each game its own server in a .mcp.json in the game's folder. Without it, one server works on one project, and the install says when it kept an existing one.
One command connects Claude Code to a project. The agent sees takes as pictures and uses the same steps you do. Downloads, deleting and extensions stay in your hands.
Every tool is in the MCP reference. To have the agent judge shader looks: a shader from a description.

The agent has no Gen Studio tools: run gen mcp install again and read what it prints, then start a new session. It works on the wrong project: see Several games above. A step it started failed: it's the same queue. See use the queue and troubleshooting.

You set Gen Studio up, learn where things are in the window, and make one picture: the concept art of a market cart, with two takes to choose from. About 10 minutes, plus the downloads, which run in the background. You'll make: a project for a small game: a mountain village during its lantern festival the concept picture of a market cart You'll learn: what the setup window asks the four words the app uses: asset, step, take, in use how to make a take, make another, and pick one Every tutorial in the path adds to this same project, so by the end you have a village's worth of assets in Godot.
Linux and an NVIDIA GPU. What else you need, and how to install, is in set up Gen Studio. Free disk space: 80 GB for the Minimal tier, 266 GB for Recommended.

Start the app with gen-app. The Set up Gen Studio window opens over it. Press Express. It takes the suggestion for this machine and shows the plan: where models go, the tier, and how much downloads. Start the install, then press Continue in background. The downloads carry on while you use the app, and after a restart too. Checkpoint the setup window is closed and you see Home. The bottom bar shows a download running. A kind of asset works as soon as its models arrive, and props come first. If you closed the window with Not now, Home shows a Finish setup row that opens it again.

A project is a folder that holds your assets, usually one per game. On Home, under Projects, press New project…. Pick PS3 as the Target look. The target look is the era your game looks like. It sets the polygon and texture budgets, and you can change it later in Settings → Project. Press Choose the folder… and pick an empty folder, for example ~/gen/lantern-village. Checkpoint Home shows your project's name, a prompt bar, and Latest takes with nothing in it yet.

Home answers "what's happening, and what needs me?". Latest takes shows your newest results, Waiting for you lists what can't go on without you, and On the GPU shows the running job. Assets in the top bar (Ctrl+2) lists everything in the project. Settings is at the top right (Ctrl+,). Queue, at the right end of the bottom bar, lists what's running and what's waiting. One big model runs at a time, so jobs wait their turn. Four words come up everywhere: An asset is one thing you make: a prop, a character, a sound. A step is one stage of making it. A prop's first step is Concept, a picture. A take is one try at a step. Takes stay until you discard them. The take in use is the one the next step builds from. The tour has every screen.

Press All kinds… on Home (or Ctrl+N). The New asset window opens. Under From a description, pick Props & scenery, then 3D prop. The right side shows the steps a prop runs and its form. Write this in Prompt: a small wooden market cart with a striped canvas awning and crates of potion bottles Type market_cart in Asset name, or press the sparkle beside it for a name made from the prompt. Press Generate. Checkpoint the asset opens as a tab. The rail at the top has one step, Concept, and its dot shows it's running. When it finishes, the picture fills the middle and Take 1 sits in the strip below. A new asset runs its first step, then waits for you.

Press Retake (or R). A second take starts with a new seed. Take 1 stays where it is, and stays in use. When Take 2 is done, click each take in the strip to compare them. ← and → move between them. Click the one you like better. If it isn't the one in use, the green button in the bar above the picture reads Use and run Prepped cut-out. Don't press it yet: that would also start the next step, and the next tutorial does that with another prop. To use a take without running on, double-click it in the strip. Checkpoint the strip has two takes and the one you chose is marked in use. Back on Home, Latest takes shows the cart.

Setup downloads in the background, and each kind works when its models arrive. A project is a folder with a target look. An asset is a row of steps. Each step has takes, and one take is in use. Retake adds a take. It never replaces one.
Your first prop: a lantern, from the concept to a game mesh in Godot.

"Needs a download" or "not installed": the step's model hasn't arrived yet. See troubleshooting. "Ran out of GPU memory": close what else uses the GPU, or see troubleshooting. The setup stopped part way: set up Gen Studio says how to run it again. A job seems stuck: use the queue.

You make a brass lantern: concept art, a 3D model, a game mesh inside your target look's budget, and then the file in a Godot project. About 15 minutes, most of it waiting for the models. You'll make: lantern, a prop with a baked texture, as a .glb in Godot You'll learn: a prop's steps: Concept, Prepped cut-out, Mesh, Game mesh Use and run, Run to end and Re-run stale the big 3D viewer Export to Godot

Do first launch: you need the project from it. A Godot 4 project somewhere on disk: a folder with project.godot. An empty new project is fine. Blender on your PATH. The Game mesh step uses it, and gen doctor says whether it's found.

Press All kinds… on Home (or Ctrl+N), then Props & scenery and 3D prop. Write this in Prompt: a brass alchemist's lantern with blue glass panes and a ring handle Type lantern in Asset name. Press Generate. Say what it is, what it's made of and how worn it is. The camera and the plain background are added for you. The sparkle on the prompt rewrites it the way the step's model likes it. Checkpoint the lantern opens with one step on the rail, Concept, and its first take appears in the middle. From the command line, in the project folder, this does the same and runs every step: gen make prop "a brass alchemist's lantern with blue glass panes and a ring handle" --asset lantern --seed 5

Fixing a shape in the picture is quicker than fixing it in 3D, so get the concept right first. Press Retake once or twice. Each take gets a new seed, and the old ones stay. Click through the takes in the strip. Look for a clean outline, all four sides plausible, and nothing fused to the lantern. Click the take you want, then press Use and run Prepped cut-out. It makes this take the one in use and starts the next step from it. If your choice is already in use, the button isn't there: go straight on to Run to end. Checkpoint a second pill, Prepped cut-out, is on the rail. It shows the lantern cut out of its background.

Press Run to end in the toolbar. Watch the rail. New steps appear as they start: Mesh builds a dense 3D model from the cut-out. This is the long one. Game mesh rebuilds it inside your target look's triangle budget and bakes the texture. While it runs, press Queue in the bottom bar to see what's running and what waits. Checkpoint the rail reads Concept, Prepped cut-out, Mesh, Game mesh, each with a finished dot. Nothing is marked stale.

Click Game mesh on the rail, then Open large (or double-click the model). Drag to turn it, scroll to zoom. Press 3 for the wireframe, 7 for the UV checker and 1 to go back to shaded. H puts a 1.8 m figure beside it for scale. Read the side panel: Stats and Budget show the triangles against what the target look allows. Turn it in 3D the lantern's game mesh Not happy with it? Go back to Concept and use another take. The steps built from the old one turn stale: still there, but out of date. Re-run stale in the toolbar rebuilds them. To change only the mesh, set Triangle budget or Texture size on Game mesh and press Retake. Checkpoint the model in the viewer looks like your concept from every side, and the budget isn't exceeded.

Press Export to Godot in the toolbar. The first time, pick your Godot project's folder, the one that holds project.godot. Gen Studio remembers it. Shift-click the button to pick another. Open the project in Godot. The lantern is in res://assets/gen/lantern/. Drag the .glb into a 3D scene. gen export lantern ~/games/lantern-village Checkpoint the lantern stands in your Godot scene with its texture.

A prop is four steps, and each is built from the take in use of the one before. Use and run picks a take and goes on. Run to end does the rest. Changing the take in use makes later steps stale, and Re-run stale rebuilds them. Export copies the takes in use into res://assets/gen/<asset>/. Export again after a retake and the files are replaced in place.
A character that moves: the same steps, plus a skeleton and a walk.

Parts are missing from the model (the ring handle, thin bars): see troubleshooting. It looks wrong in Godot: see troubleshooting. Export refuses: stale steps or the wrong folder. See troubleshooting and export to Godot. More on takes: retake and compare and run the stale steps.

You export everything from the earlier tutorials in one go, add the Gen Studio dock to the Godot editor, and build a small scene: the courier walking on a cobbled street beside a lantern, a pond, a blue flame, with the theme playing. About 15 minutes. You'll make: one Godot scene that uses a prop, a character, a texture, a shader, an effect, sounds and music You'll learn: exporting a whole project at once, and what lands where the dock: the queue and Import inside the editor that a retake reaches your scene by exporting again

The assets from your first prop, a character that moves, textures, shaders and effects and sound and music. You can follow along with fewer. A Godot 4 project: a folder with project.godot. No stale steps. Export refuses a stale asset, so Godot never gets a half-updated model.

In Gen Studio, press Assets in the top bar (Ctrl+2). On the left, click Stale. If anything is listed, open it and press Re-run stale. Click Not exported to see what Godot doesn't have yet. Go to Home (Ctrl+1) and press Export to Godot. It exports every finished asset that isn't stale. Checkpoint in Godot's FileSystem panel, res://assets/gen/ has one folder per asset. In res://assets/gen/ What's inside lantern/ the Game mesh .glb courier/ the rig .glb, with every clip inside cobblestone/ the maps and material.tres pond_water/ the .gdshader blue_flame/ the sprite sheet and its materials bottle_clink/, door_creak/, village_theme/ .ogg files; the track has its loop points set market_dialogue/ Dialogue Manager files From a terminal it's one asset at a time: gen export lantern ~/games/lantern-village gen export courier ~/games/lantern-village

The dock is a small editor plug-in. It shows the queue and imports finished assets. It makes nothing itself. Install it into the Godot project: gen dock install ~/games/lantern-village Start the server for your Gen Studio project, and leave it running: gen serve --project ~/gen/lantern-village Reopen the game in Godot. The Gen Studio dock appears and says Connected. Find lantern under Assets and press Import beside it. It does what Export to Godot does, from this side. Checkpoint the dock lists your assets with their kinds, and none is marked stale. The dock keeps the server's address and a token in addons/gen_studio/server.json. Don't commit that file to a public repository: the token lets anyone on your network use the queue.

These steps are in the Godot editor. Make a new 3D scene and save it as village.tscn. Add a MeshInstance3D with a PlaneMesh for the street. Drag cobblestone/material.tres onto it. Add a second, smaller plane for the pond. Give it a new ShaderMaterial and set its shader to the .gdshader in pond_water/. The shader's uniforms show as sliders in the inspector. Drag the lantern's .glb and the courier's .glb into the scene, and stand them on the street. Select the courier's AnimationPlayer and play the walk. Clips whose names end in _loop loop. Add a GPUParticles3D for the flame and give it the particle material from blue_flame/. Checkpoint you see the street, the pond rippling, the lantern, the courier walking on the spot, and the flame. Now the sound: Add an AudioStreamPlayer, set its stream to the .ogg in village_theme/, and turn on Autoplay. The loop points are already in the file. Add an AudioStreamPlayer3D near the lantern. Give it an AudioStreamRandomizer and add the variants from bottle_clink/ to it. Each play picks one, so it doesn't sound the same twice. Run the scene. Checkpoint the theme plays and loops, and the scene looks like the picture at the top.

Back in Gen Studio, open lantern, go to Game mesh and press Retake with a different Triangle budget. Use the new take, then press Export to Godot, or Import in the dock. Checkpoint the lantern in village.tscn changed without you touching the scene. Export replaces the files in place, so scenes that use them pick up the change.

Export to Godot on Home does the whole project, and res://assets/gen/<asset>/ is where each asset lands. The dock is the same export, from inside the editor. Your scenes point at files that Gen Studio replaces, so a retake is an export away.
Work faster: the same things from a terminal, a batch overnight, and an agent.

Export refuses: stale steps, or the wrong folder. See troubleshooting. The model looks wrong in Godot: see troubleshooting. The dock says "not reachable", or doesn't show: the Godot dock has its own troubleshooting. What each exported file is: export to Godot and Godot scripts.

You film yourself doing a move and put it on your character as a clip. About 5 minutes, plus the filming. You'll make: a clip on the courier, from your own video You'll learn: how to film for motion capture where a video goes in New clip what makes a clip loop and stay in place
A rigged character: the courier from a character that moves. The motion-capture model: GEM-X at Balanced, SAM 3D Body at Quality. The app asks before it downloads one.

Stand the phone somewhere still, with your whole body in frame. Use a plain background if you can. Film about 5 seconds. Side-on for walks, front-on for gestures. Wear fitted clothes. Baggy ones that hide the knees track worse. Trim the video to the move. The start and the end matter for loops. Checkpoint a short video file with one move in it, head to feet visible throughout.

Copy the video into your project folder, for example as refs/wave.mp4. Open the courier and press ⋮, then New clip. Type wave in Clip name. Type the video's path, relative to the project, in Or a video file (motion capture): refs/wave.mp4. Press Generate. Checkpoint a new clip row appears on the rail. Its step tracks your body in the video, then retargets the motion to the courier's skeleton. From the command line it's a job file: # wave.yaml, run with: gen run wave.yaml asset: courier kind: mocap clip: wave video: refs/wave.mp4

Click the clip on the rail and press Open large. Press play, or drag the timeline. Bones shows the skeleton. If the feet slide or an arm is lost, film again with the whole body in frame, and retake. Checkpoint the courier does your move, on the spot. A clip loops and stays in place by default: the end meets the start, and the hips don't wander. To change that, make the clip from a job file with loop: false or in_place: false.
Motion capture from a plain video. What makes a clip loop and stay in place.
Sound and music in the learning path, or a base body and an outfit.
The clip slides, or the feet float: see troubleshooting. "Needs a download": see troubleshooting.

You turn on the pixel pack and make a small retro set: a potion sprite, a knight, a key icon, a sheet of meadow tiles, an overworld tune and a coin sound. The pictures are true pixels on a limited palette, not a big picture made to look blocky. About 15 minutes. You'll make: potion, tiny_knight and brass_key: sprites at their real size, with enlarged previews meadow_tiles, a tile sheet with one palette overworld, a chip-flavoured track, and coin, a retro sound effect You'll learn: the two steps of every pixel picture: the drawing, then Pixelate that Pixelate runs no model, so sizes and palettes are quick to try the two ways to chip music

Do first launch and your first prop. The pixel pack, gen.pixel, ships off. Turn it on in Settings → Extensions, then restart the app. Or: gen ext enable gen.pixel Its models download the first time a step needs them, after the app asks.

Press All kinds…, then Pixel art & chiptune and Pixel sprite. Write this in Sprite: a round glass potion bottle with glowing blue liquid and a cork Type potion in Asset name and press Generate. One subject, plainly described. The pixel-art style and the plain background are added for you. The first step, Drawing, is a normal-sized picture in a pixel style. Retake it until the shape is right. Press Use and run Pixelate, or Run next: Pixelate in the ⋯ menu when the take is already in use. Checkpoint the rail reads Drawing, Pixelate. The Pixelate take is the bottle cropped to its outline on a transparent background.

Pixelate works on the CPU and takes seconds, so try things here instead of redrawing. On Pixelate, set Size to 32 px and press Retake. Size is the longest side in real pixels. 48 keeps most drawings readable, 32 suits simple subjects. Set Palette to PICO-8 and retake again. A fixed palette matches each colour to the console's nearest one. Go back to Free (from the drawing) and lower Colours to 8. Small bright accents stay in the palette. Tick two or three takes in the strip and press Compare 3 (the button counts what you ticked) to see them side by side. Use the one you want. Checkpoint several Pixelate takes of the same drawing, each a different size or palette. Clean outline makes a dark outline continuous and one pixel wide. It adds none to a drawing without one. In the take's folder, sprite.png is the real-size picture for your game and preview.png is the same one enlarged. In Godot, set the texture filter to Nearest.

The other picture kinds are the same two steps. Pixel character, a full body. Name it tiny_knight: a small knight with a red plume, silver armour, round shield and short sword, front view Pixel icon, for items and UI. Name it brass_key: an ornate brass key with a heart-shaped bow Pixel tiles, a sheet cut at the tiles' borders, 16 or 32 px, with one palette. Name it meadow_tiles: grass meadow with a dirt path, small flowers and stones, top-down Checkpoint four pixel assets in the project, each with a Drawing and its pixel version. # knight.yaml, run with: gen run knight.yaml asset: tiny_knight kind: pixel_character prompt: a small knight with a red plume, silver armour, round shield and short sword, front view

Press All kinds…, then Pixel art & chiptune and Chiptune. Write the mood and use in Style. The chip's tags are added for you. cheerful overworld theme, bouncy lead, driving bass, adventure Leave Sound on NES. Set Length (seconds) to 45 and BPM to 150. Type overworld in Asset name and press Generate. Now the coin: Retro sound effect, with Sound on coin. Name it coin and press Generate. No model runs: a generator makes it in a moment. Play the coin's variants and press Pick this one on the ones you keep. The first is the classic sound, the others are close relatives. the overworld theme Checkpoint a looping track that sounds like an old console, and a coin sound with four variants. The Chiptune step asks a music model to imitate a console. For the real chip voices, take any Music track, add Stems, then MIDI, then Chip render: it keeps the song and changes the band, playing the notes on the Era you pick. Crush on a chiptune makes it harsher and closer to the hardware.

A pixel picture is drawn large, then reduced to real pixels and a palette. Retake Pixelate, not the drawing, to change size, colours or palette. Chiptune imitates a console, Chip render plays real chip voices from a track's notes, and retro sounds come from a generator.
An anime character with sprites and a 2D rig, or put the sprites in a game: export to Godot.

The pixel kinds don't show in New asset: the pack is off, or the app wasn't restarted. See extensions on and off. "Needs a download": see troubleshooting. The sprite looks blurry in Godot: set the texture filter to Nearest. Chip render's notes land off the beat: set BPM on the step yourself. See stems and MIDI.

You describe a shader in a sentence and get a .gdshader that compiles in Godot, with sliders for what you want to tweak. Then you read the judge's notes and steer a retake. About 5 minutes. You'll make: a flickering green witchlight glow, as a .gdshader with uniforms You'll learn: what to put in the description the compile loop and the judge rounds how to let Claude Code be the judge
Textures, shaders and effects makes a first shader. This page goes further with one. Godot 4 installed: the step compiles in it.

Press All kinds…, then Shader. Say where it goes, what it looks like and what you want to change later, in Describe the shader: a flickering green witchlight glow with a soft pulsing core and a thin bright rim; tweakable colour and pulse speed Name it witchlight and press Generate. Checkpoint the Shader step is running. Fast takes about a minute. Balanced and Quality take about four, because they judge the look too.

Watch the step. The text model writes the shader and Godot compiles it. Compile errors go back to the model until it compiles. At Balanced and Quality, the model then looks at a render and fixes what's missing: up to eight rounds. Each round gets the notes of the rounds before. When it's done, read the take. It keeps the best-scored round. Open the take's folder and read judge.json: every round's score and notes. judge/N.png is each round's preview. Checkpoint the take shows code and a preview. In the code, each uniform with a hint_range is a slider in Godot's inspector.

Read the judge's last notes. They say what's still missing. Rewrite the description to name it: the surface (2D sprite or 3D mesh), the colours, what moves, and the uniforms you want (with a uniform for the rim colour). Press Retake. Checkpoint a second take whose preview is closer. Both takes stay, and you choose which is in use. Under Advanced, Fix rounds sets how many times the model may fix compile errors before giving up. Use an example from Godot Shaders passes the closest free shader to the model as a reference.

Press Export to Godot. Make a ShaderMaterial on your mesh or sprite and pick the .gdshader. Set its uniforms in the inspector. Checkpoint the witchlight glows on your mesh, and the sliders change it live.
With Settings → Extensions → Who reviews a shader's look set to Claude Code, a take waits for Claude Code's verdict instead of the text model's. See Claude Code over MCP.
Shaders written and compiled for you, with sliders. The judge rounds, and how to steer a retake.
A base body and an outfit, or Claude Code over MCP.

It never compiles: raise Fix rounds, or say less in one shader. A failed job's panel has its log (Copy log). The look is wrong but it compiles: that's the Fast profile, which doesn't judge. Retake at Balanced. Anything else: troubleshooting.

You give the village its sound: two sound effects with variants, a looping theme, and a waltz written note by note that you can edit bar by bar. Then you clean one sound up and run it through effects. About 15 minutes. You'll make: bottle_clink and door_creak, sound effects with several variants each village_theme, a 60-second track that loops festival_waltz, a composed piece with a MIDI file for a DAW You'll learn: variants, and picking the ones that go on what pins a track: length, BPM, key the composer and its editor the optional Clean up and Effects steps
Do your first prop, for takes and export. Headphones or speakers. Sounds are matched in loudness, so you compare the sound and not the level.

Press All kinds…, then Sound and Sound effect. Write this in Sound: two glass potion bottles clinking together Set Length (seconds) to 1.5. Leave Variants at 4. Type bottle_clink in Asset name and press Generate. Play each variant in the take (Space plays and pauses). Press Pick this one on the ones you keep. The button then reads Picked. Make door_creak the same way, at 2.5 seconds: an old wooden door creaking open the bottle clink, one variant Checkpoint two sound assets, each with one take of four variants and at least one picked. Variants are a round robin: the same sound, each nudged a little in pitch and level, so it doesn't sound the same twice in your game. Describe the source and the action, and keep it to one event. The steps after this one go on with the variants you picked.

Press All kinds…, then Sound and Music. Write tags in Style: genre, mood, instruments. cozy mountain village theme, hammered dulcimer, pizzicato strings and a soft flute, warm and hopeful, instrumental Set Length (seconds) to 60 and BPM to 96. Leave Seamless loop on. Open Advanced and set Key to G major. Type village_theme in Asset name and press Generate. Play the take, then press L to loop it and listen across the join. Checkpoint the take's waveform has its loop points marked, and the join is hard to hear. Seamless loop finds a loop point and cuts the track to it, on whole bars. Leave Lyrics empty for an instrumental. From here, Add step offers Stems (drums, bass, vocals and the rest) and then MIDI: see stems and MIDI. # village_theme.yaml, run with: gen run village_theme.yaml asset: village_theme kind: music seed: 12 prompt: cozy mountain village theme, hammered dulcimer, pizzicato strings and a soft flute, warm and hopeful, instrumental bpm: 96 duration: 60 keyscale: G major

The Music step makes audio. The composer writes notes: rules and tables, no model, nothing on the GPU, done in seconds. You get a .mid for a DAW and a preview to hear. Press All kinds…, then Sound and Composed music. Set Style to Gentle town: a light major tune for flute, clarinet and piano. Type festival_waltz in Asset name and press Generate. The seed picks the key, tempo, form and ending. With Seed at 14 and Random seed off you get the piece on these pages. Play the take. Then press Edit on it to open the composer's editor. Click an instrument's notes in one bar, then press New idea. It's a fresh draw of only what you picked, listed under Takes with the changed notes lit. Pick the one to keep, or go back to Current. Press Save as new take. Nothing changes until you do, and the take you opened stays as it was. the festival waltz Checkpoint the Compose step has two takes: the first draw, and yours with one bar changed. Rework rhythm and Rework pitches vary notes that are already there, and Notes is a piano roll where you draw your own. Edit a composed piece covers the editor.

Both steps are optional and sit after the sound. Try them on the door. Open door_creak and press Add step at the end of the rail. Pick Clean up. Leave Strength on Normal and Shimmer on Auto, and press New take. Each sound is measured first, and only what the measurements show gets fixed. Press Add step again and pick Effects. The middle of this step is the mixer. Open Quick setup in the inputs, choose a Room, and press Fill the rack. What you hear is live. Press New take to render the rack into a take. Checkpoint the door's rail reads Sound effect, Clean up, Effects. The Effects take sounds like the door in a room. Role on the Effects step sets the loudness the sound is delivered at and whether it's mono (placed in 3D) or stereo. More in clean up a recording and the mixer and layers.

A sound effect is several variants, and you pick which go on. Music is audio from tags, with loop points. Composed music is notes from rules, which you can edit. Clean up fixes, Effects shapes, and neither changes the take they started from.
Voices and words: a shopkeeper's voice, a haggling scene, and an item's text.
A sound has hiss or a metallic shimmer: clean up a recording. The loop's join is easy to hear: retake the Music step. "Needs a download": see troubleshooting. Anything else: troubleshooting.

You make three things that aren't models: a cobblestone texture that tiles, with its maps and a Godot material; a pond-water shader that Godot compiles; and a blue flame as an animated flipbook. About 15 minutes.
