You'll make: cobblestone, a tiling texture with a normal map, roughness and a material.tres pond_water, a .gdshader with sliders blue_flame, a sprite sheet with particle materials You'll learn: what the target look changes on a texture how a shader is written, compiled and judged an effect's two steps: the still, then the motion
Do your first prop, so you know takes, Run to end and export. Godot 4 installed: the Shader step compiles in it. The project's target look at PS3 or PS4. PBR maps are made from PS3 up.

Press All kinds…, then Props & scenery and Texture tile. Write this in Surface: worn cobblestone street with moss between the stones Type cobblestone in Asset name and press Generate. Look at the take. Say the material, its colours and its wear. The app asks for a flat, evenly lit surface and fixes the seams itself. When you have a tile you like, press Run to end. PBR maps runs next and stops for review. Checkpoint the rail reads Texture, PBR maps. The maps take shows the tile, a normal map and a roughness map. The target look decides how the tile is finished. At PS1 and PS2 it's reduced to a palette and has no PBR maps. PS3 and PS4 keep full colour and add the maps. PS4 also offers an Upscale step. # cobblestone.yaml, run with: gen run cobblestone.yaml asset: cobblestone kind: texture prompt: worn cobblestone street with moss between the stones

Press All kinds…, then Shader on the left and Shader in the middle. Write this in Describe the shader: calm pond water with gentle ripples and soft highlights that scroll slowly Type pond_water in Asset name and press Generate. Watch the step. The text model writes the shader and Godot compiles it. Compile errors go back to the model until it compiles. At Balanced and Quality, the model then looks at a render of the shader and fixes what's missing, for up to eight rounds. The take keeps the best-scored round. This is why Balanced takes minutes where Fast takes about one. Checkpoint the take shows the code and a preview of rippling water. The code has uniform lines. Each uniform with a hint_range becomes a slider in Godot's inspector. To get the sliders you want, name them in the description: with a uniform for the ripple speed. Say where the shader goes too: a 3D surface, a 2D sprite, or the sky. Then Retake. Shader goes deeper: the judge's notes, and letting Claude Code be the judge.

Press All kinds…, then Effects and Effect. Write this in Effect: a burst of blue magic flame with sparks Type blue_flame in Asset name and press Generate. The first step, Effect, draws one clean still on black. Retake until the still is right. The motion is built from it, so this is the cheap place to fix the shape and colours. Press Run to end. Animated effect has a video model animate the still, then cuts the frames into a sprite sheet. To steer the motion, click Animated effect, write what happens over time in How it moves, for example flares up, the flames curl and fade to sparks, and press Retake. For a steady fire or an aura, turn on Loop: the last frames blend into the first. the blue flame's flipbook Checkpoint the rail reads Effect, Animated effect. The take plays the flame and shows its sprite sheet. Length (seconds) goes up to 5. Longer takes longer to make: 5 seconds is about two and a half times 2 seconds. Add step at the end of the rail offers Effect sound, a sound made in sync with the clip, in variants.

Open each asset and press Export to Godot. Or go to Home and press Export to Godot there: it exports every finished asset that isn't stale. In Godot, look in res://assets/gen/: cobblestone/ has the maps and material.tres. Put the material on a mesh. pond_water/ has the .gdshader. Make a ShaderMaterial on a mesh and pick it. blue_flame/ has the sprite sheet and its particle materials. Checkpoint three new folders are in res://assets/gen/. You use them in a small scene in Godot.

A texture's later steps depend on the target look. A shader take is code that already compiles, with sliders for what you named. An effect is a still, then a flipbook made from it. Fix the still first.
Sound and music: bottles, a door, and the village's theme.

The Shader step fails or never compiles: gen doctor checks the runtimes. A failed job's panel has its log (Copy log). See troubleshooting. "Needs a download": see troubleshooting. "Ran out of GPU memory" on Animated effect: see troubleshooting. A prompt isn't landing: write better prompts.

You design a voice for the village's potion seller, write a haggling scene as a dialogue file for Godot, write an item's text, and then have the scene spoken line by line. About 10 minutes. You'll make: shopkeeper_voice, a voice you can reuse for every line that character says market_dialogue, a scene with stable keys, as a Dialogue Manager file moonwater_tonic, an item's name, description, flavour and stats the scene's lines as sound files, with lip-sync shapes You'll learn: a voice is an asset, made once and then used by other assets text steps stop for review before anything is built on them how Voice lines joins a dialogue and its voices
Do your first prop, for takes and Add step. The text and voice models. If one isn't installed, the app asks before it downloads.

Press All kinds…, then Sound and Voice. Write this in The voice: a cheerful young shopkeeper, bright warm voice, a little fast Leave Language on English. Type shopkeeper_voice in Asset name and press Generate. Play the take. It's a short reference clip of the voice saying a sample line. If it isn't the character, write more and press Retake. The field's help asks for 40 to 80 words: age, pitch, accent, pace, texture, mood and how they speak. the shopkeeper's voice Checkpoint one asset with one step, Voice, and a take you like in use. That take is the reference every line is spoken from, so choose it before you voice anything.

Press All kinds…, then Writing and Dialogue. Write what happens in The scene: who talks, where, and how it ends. A potion seller haggles with a travelling swordswoman who only has three copper coins Write the speakers in Characters, as they're named in your game: Pell, Rin. Leave Lines at 10. Type market_dialogue in Asset name and press Generate. Read the take. Each line has its speaker and a stable key, so you can retake a translation or a voice later without your game's references moving. Checkpoint the Dialogue step shows the scene. The run stopped here: a dialogue is a review, because the steps after it are built from these exact words. If your project has a lore/ folder, its files are passed to the text model, so names and facts stay the same from one asset to the next.

Press All kinds…, then Writing and Item. Write this in What is the item?: Moonwater tonic: a pale blue potion brewed from snowmelt gathered under a full moon, restores stamina Set Rarity to rare. It changes the tone and the stats. Type moonwater_tonic in Asset name and press Generate. Checkpoint the Item text step shows a name, a description, flavour text and stats. On disk it's checked JSON, ready for your game to read. To translate it, press Continue: the Translations step runs with Languages set to es. Write other codes there, separated by commas, and press Retake. A dialogue translates the same way. gen make item "Moonwater tonic: a pale blue potion brewed from snowmelt gathered under a full moon, restores stamina" --asset moonwater_tonic

Open market_dialogue and press Add step at the end of the rail. Pick Voice lines. In Voices, give each speaker a voice asset, as Speaker = voice asset, separated by commas: Pell=shopkeeper_voice, Rin=shopkeeper_voice Press New take. Every line is spoken in its speaker's voice and levelled. Play a few lines. Checkpoint the Voice lines take lists the ten lines, each with a waveform. Each line also has lip-sync shapes as JSON for Godot. Both speakers share one voice here, to keep the tutorial short. For a real scene, make a second Voice asset for Rin the way you made the first, and put its name after Rin=. Voices are designed in ten languages. For Japanese there are also free AivisHub voices: see find free assets. gen retake market_dialogue voice_lines --set "voices=Pell=shopkeeper_voice, Rin=shopkeeper_voice"

Press Export to Godot on the dialogue and on the item. In Godot, res://assets/gen/market_dialogue/ has the Dialogue Manager files. Checkpoint the dialogue file opens in Godot. Playing it needs the Dialogue Manager add-on in your Godot project.

A voice is designed once, then named in Voices wherever it speaks. Text kinds stop for review after the writing. Continue runs the translations. Keys stay stable, so text, translations and voices can each be retaken alone. Three more kinds in Writing work the same way: Barks (short lines for idle, combat, hurt and victory), Names, and Lore check, which compares any text with your lore files.
A small scene in Godot: everything you've made so far, in one place.
"Needs a download": see troubleshooting. A line is read wrong: retake the Voice lines step, or retake the voice with a longer description. Anything else: troubleshooting.

You make one plain body, dress it in pieces that fit over each other, save them as an outfit, and swap outfits at runtime in Godot. About 60 minutes for the body and four pieces. Most of that is the model and rig steps, which run without you. You'll make: base_body, a rigged body that clothes fit onto four wearables: a shirt, a coat, boots and a cape a travel outfit, and the script that puts it on in Godot You'll learn: slots and layers, and why inner layers are made first the Wardrobe window wardrobe.gd in Godot
documents.s: A base body and an outfit

documents.t: Do a character that moves: a base body runs a character's steps. To add one piece to a character you already have, skip the body: a wearable fits any character with a Rig step. The sample project's courier_hat is made that way for courier.

Press All kinds…, then Characters & bodies and Base body. Choose what the body wears: underwear, a plain bodysuit or a mannequin. Write this in Prompt: a slim adult base body in plain grey underwear, neutral face, short dark hair, barefoot Type base_body in Asset name and press Generate. Run it like a character: choose a concept, check the Turnaround, press Run to end, review the Rig and press Continue. Checkpoint the rail reads Concept, Turnaround, High poly, Game mesh, Rig. The concept keeps the shapes clean (bare feet, short hair) so clothes fit onto them. # base_body.yaml, run with: gen run base_body.yaml asset: base_body kind: body base: underwear prompt: a slim adult base body in plain grey underwear, neutral face, short dark hair, barefoot

On the body, press ⋮ in the toolbar, then Wardrobe. Press New piece. It opens New asset on Wearable, for this body. Write one piece in The piece: a white linen shirt. Name it shirt and press Generate. The first step, Design, is a review: it draws the piece on the body. Check it, then press Continue. Mesh, Fit, Paint and Skin follow. Make the others the same way, one at a time and in this order: a long leather coat, leather boots, a short wool cape. Checkpoint four wearable assets, each fitted and skinned to the body's skeleton. Slot and Layer are Auto. The coat is outer torso on layer 2, so it's fitted over the shirt on layer 1. Make the inner layers first: a piece is fitted over what exists when it's made. A cape gets bone chains so it swings.

Open the body and press ⋮, then Wardrobe. Each piece shows its slot, its layer and what it was fitted over. Read the top of the window. A clash, two pieces in one slot and layer, is flagged there. Check the pieces you want together. Type travel in Save the checked pieces as and press Save outfit. Checkpoint travel is listed under Outfits, as in the picture at the top. gen outfit base_body travel shirt coat boots cape

Press Export to Godot on the body and on each piece. Put the body's .glb in a scene and name the node Body. Add a script that dresses it: const Wardrobe := preload("res://assets/gen/wardrobe.gd") func _ready() -> void: Wardrobe.wear_outfit($Body, "res://assets/gen/base_body/outfits.json", "travel") Wardrobe.unequip($Body, "back") # the cape off Run the scene. Checkpoint the body wears the shirt, coat and boots, and the cape is off. One piece per slot is worn: putting one on takes off what was in its slot. The body under what's worn is hidden, so it can't poke through.
A base body that clothes fit onto. Pieces in slots and layers, fitted over each other. Outfits, and swapping them in Godot.
A clip from your phone: clips play on the body, and the clothes follow. Why it works this way: how wearables, fitting and cloth work.
A piece pokes through the body: see troubleshooting. The cape doesn't move, or explodes: see troubleshooting and cloth presets. The functions of wardrobe.gd: Godot scripts.

You do what the earlier tutorials did without the window: one asset from a terminal, a file of jobs that runs overnight, and an agent that makes, looks and picks for you. About 15 minutes at the keyboard. The batch runs while you're away. You'll make: market_cart, taken from its concept to a game mesh with gen a batch file that makes more of the village while you sleep a Claude Code session that can drive your project You'll learn: the commands behind the buttons: make, run, status, retake, promote, run-to, export job files and batch files what an agent may and may not do

The project from the earlier tutorials. Run the commands from its folder, or add --project <folder>. For the last section: Claude Code installed. The CLI uses the ids from files and folders. A step goes by its id (Game mesh is retopo, Rig is skin), and Take 3 is v003 or just 3. The app says target look where files say fidelity.

See where the cart from first launch stands: gen status market_cart It lists each step's takes, the one in use, and anything stale. Make one more concept take with a changed prompt: gen <Term tip="A new take of a step, kept beside the others until you choose to use it." to="/docs/glossary/#retake">retake</Term> market_cart concept --prompt "a small wooden market cart with a striped canvas awning and crates of potion bottles, two large spoked wheels" A take from gen retake is kept, but not used until you promote it. Use the take you want. This is Use this take: gen promote market_cart concept 3 Build up to the game mesh. This is Run to here: gen run-to market_cart retopo Export it: gen export market_cart ~/games/lantern-village Checkpoint gen status market_cart shows every step up to retopo with a take in use and nothing stale. The app shows the same thing: both read the project's folders. --set changes any field of a step's form by its key, for example gen retake market_cart retopo --set triangles=2000. The keys are in steps and fields. A new asset can come from gen make, for a prop, character, music, item or mesh, or from a job file, for any kind: # door.yaml, run with: gen run door.yaml asset: door_creak kind: sfx prompt: an old wooden door creaking open seconds: 2.5 A job runs from the kind's first step to its first review, or to the end when it has none.

A batch is many jobs in one file. It runs at low priority, behind anything you queue by hand. Make a batches/ folder in the project and write batches/overnight.yaml: jobs: # plain jobs, as in a job file - {asset: oak_planks, kind: texture, prompt: "old oak floor planks with visible grain and nail heads"} - {asset: guard_barks, kind: barks, prompt: "a sleepy gate guard of a mountain village during the lantern festival"} matrix: # every combination of the list-valued fields kind: prop asset: "{prompt}_{seed}" # a name pattern prompt: [a wooden market stall, a stone well, a paper festival lantern] <Term tip="The number that fixes a model's random choices, so the same seed with the same settings gives the same result." to="/docs/glossary/#seed">seed</Term>: [1, 2] <Term tip="How long a step may take (Ultra fast, Fast, Balanced or Quality), which picks the model and its settings." to="/docs/glossary/#profile">profile</Term>: [fast] Run it: gen batch batches/overnight.yaml The whole file is checked first: if one job is wrong, nothing is queued. Leave it. Jobs that use the same model run one after another, so the model isn't reloaded between them. Checkpoint the terminal reports each step as it finishes. The matrix makes 3 prompts × 2 seeds = 6 props, with names like a_stone_well_2. Start small: one prompt and one seed, to check the file. Use a fast profile for a night of ideas, then retake the best at Quality. If the machine stops part way, the job that was cut off goes back in the queue. Pick up with: gen queue run Don't run gen batch again: that queues the whole file a second time. To watch from the sofa, run gen serve --project . and open the printed URL on your phone. It shows recent takes, progress and the GPU, and can pause the queue or start a file from batches/.

Add Gen Studio to Claude Code: gen <Term tip="The Model Context Protocol, which lets an agent such as Claude Code drive Gen Studio through the gen-mcp server." to="/docs/glossary/#mcp">mcp</Term> install --project ~/gen/lantern-village This adds the gen-studio MCP server and a skill that tells the agent how to use it. Start a new Claude Code session and ask for something with a judgement in it: Make a prop: a hanging paper lantern with a brass cap. Show me two takes of the concept, use the better one, run it to the game mesh and export it to ~/games/lantern-village. Watch it work. It starts jobs and waits for them, looks at takes as pictures, compares them, uses one, runs on, checks Godot's import and exports. Checkpoint a new prop is in the project and in Godot, and the agent told you which take it used and why. What an agent can't do on its own: It asks you before a download. Deleting only moves steps and takes to the project's .trash, and needs a confirmation. Extensions and library folders are yours. It tells you the command. Claude Code over MCP has more, and every tool is in the MCP reference.

Every button has a command, and the app and the CLI share one project and one queue. A batch is a file of jobs, with a matrix for combinations, that survives a crash. An agent sees takes and makes the same choices you would, inside limits.
You've finished the path. More to try, in any order: an anime character, pixel art and chiptune, a base body and an outfit, a clip from your phone, a shader, in depth.

"not installed" from a command: the CLI refuses a step whose model is missing and prints the command: gen install weights --group <group>. See troubleshooting. A batch job failed: see batches overnight and use the queue. The phone page won't open: the queue on your phone. gen doctor checks the GPU, the driver, disk space and the runtimes.

Everything about one thing, one page each. Every page has the same shape: an at-a-glance box, how it works, how to use it, its settings, tips, troubleshooting and related pages. Asset kinds: everything you can make. Steps: every step, the model each profile runs, its fields and prompt tips. Extensions: the packs of models and steps, their weights and licences. The words are in the glossary. New here? Start with the tutorials.

The packs of models and steps, their weights and licences. Turn them on and off in Settings → Extensions. gen.ace-step Game music with ACE-Step 1.5 XL turbo on ComfyUI, then loop points and loudness in its own env. gen.aivis Japanese voices from AivisHub (AivisSpeech's Style-Bert-VITS2 models, ONNX on the CPU): a voice imported from Find free assets is pinned by its file's sha256, then speaks dialogue lines with Rhubarb lip-sync. gen.anime Anime characters and 2D art on Anima (spec 013; WAI-Anima, Anima Turbo for the fast profiles): free images, characters, shots, sprite and portrait sets, facesets, reactions and backgrounds. NoobAI-XL is an add-on (gen.anime-noobai). gen.anime-noobai NoobAI-XL for the anime pack (an add-on of gen.anime, ADR-0013): every anime step as another Model, with NoobAI's own tools: IP-Adapter references, OpenPose poses, the inpainting and canny ControlNets, DMD2 for the fast profiles and the kashimu chibi LoRA. NoobAI's official quality tags and negative. gen.audio-fx The Effects rack (spec 010): an ordered chain of Pedalboard effects, real spaces (Voxengo impulse responses) and free VST3 plugins after a sound or track, in its own CPU env. Plugins run here, never in the app. gen.audio-restore Clean up's model help (spec 010): FlashSR (one-step audio super-resolution to 48 kHz) restores a dull top end at Balanced and Quality on PS3/PS4; SonicMaster (Apache-2.0) repairs and masters a track at Quality; it's optional (the Music repair bundle) because it needs Stability AI's gated VAE. Called by the Clean up step, not steps of their own. gen.chord PBR maps from a texture image with CHORD (Ubisoft La Forge): base colour, normal, roughness, metalness. Research-only licence (recorded). gen.composer A rule-based MIDI composer (spec 038): a style and a seed to a piece, with no model, a .mid for your DAW and a rendered preview, edited bar by bar. gen.concept Concept art for image-to-3D: Qwen-Image 2.1 bf16 (quality), FLUX.3 klein (balanced), Z-Image-Turbo (fast) and SDXL + DMD2 (ultra fast) on ComfyUI. gen.gem-x Motion capture from video with NVIDIA GEM-X (SOMA body, contact/IK post-processing), written as a BVH. Commercial use allowed. gen.hy-motion Text to motion with Tencent HY-Motion 1.0 via hymotion-local (Qwen3-8B text encoder offloaded to RAM): BVH at 30 fps, Mixamo bone names. gen.hy3d-paint Paint texture: Hunyuan3D-Paint 2.1 paints albedo, roughness and metallic onto a model you have (or made) from one reference image; the core bakes them back onto the original mesh, keeping its topology and rig. ~21 GB of VRAM. Tencent Hunyuan non-commercial licence (no EU/UK/KR). gen.kits Kits (spec 039): optional recipes picked on a step by a picture card. Adds no step; nothing runs or downloads until a Kit is picked. gen.momask Text to motion with MoMask (masked residual transformer, HumanML3D): a quick BVH at 20 fps. gen.moss-sfx Sound effects with MOSS-SoundEffect v2 (1.3B DiT, 48 kHz, up to 30 s) in its own env; variants by seed. The Fast recipe; Balanced and Quality are Woosh (gen.woosh). gen.pixel Pixel art and chiptune (spec 031): sprites, characters, icons and tile sheets as true pixels from the image models you have; chiptune tracks, Chip render (a track's stems replayed on NES, Genesis, SNES or PS1 chips) and retro sound effects. No new models. gen.quaternius Text to motion without a model: the closest clip from Quaternius' CC0 Universal Animation Library, by name. gen.qwen-edit Character turnarounds: Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 + multi-angle LoRA (fast, balanced) or one Qwen-Image 2.1 four-view sheet (quality), on ComfyUI core nodes; Frame in 3D, Edit with a prompt and Relight (LightingRemap). gen.qwen-tts Character voices with Qwen3-TTS 1.7B: design a voice from a description, then speak every dialogue line in it, with Rhubarb lip-sync. gen.retopo Low-poly retopology tiers (PyMeshLab, Blender Decimate, QuadriFlow) with a bake from the kept high-poly. gen.sam3d-body Motion capture from video with Meta's SAM 3D Body on ComfyUI core nodes (SAM 3.1 tracking, MoGe field of view, smoothing, BVH). gen.sfx Sound effects with Stable Audio 3 Small-SFX on ComfyUI (Ultra fast); round-robin variants, trimmed, era effects and loudness in the core. gen.stems Stems and MIDI from music (spec 012): BS-RoFormer SW splits a track into six stems; Basic Pitch turns each into MIDI and one song.mid. gen.text Game text tools on the managed llama.cpp: JSON-schema output, pydantic-validated with retries. gen.texture Seamless tiling textures on ComfyUI (the concept models plus a native seam pass), finished by fidelity in the core: CLUT and dither for PS1/PS2, normal and roughness maps for PS3, a Godot material. gen.trellis2 Image to low-poly GLB with TRELLIS.2 on ComfyUI core nodes: BiRefNet prep, decimate to budget, bake (ADR-0008). gen.unirig Rigging: SkinTokens (UniRig's successor) makes the skeleton and skin weights in one step (rig; the character pipeline's Rig step) (UniRig was removed in spec 027). gen.woosh Sound effects with Sony AI's Woosh (48 kHz): DFlow (distilled, 4 steps) at Balanced, Flow (adaptive solver) at Quality; DVFlow gives an animated effect its sound from the clip. Weights CC-BY-NC: outputs are non-commercial too.

Everything you can make, one page each. In the app, these are in New asset. Background A scene with nobody in it, at other times of day (same layout), with optional parallax layers. Anime character Define a character once (a full-body sheet and their tags); then shoot them as often as you like. Anime image An Anima drawing with its background: any characters, framing and shape. Reactions (chibi or full size) A whole drawing per expression, cut out: lively, not lined up; for chat, menus or a desktop chibi. 2D rig (cut-out animation) A transparent shot split into parts on Godot bones: breathing, sway and a head tilt, hair that swings. Sprite or portrait set One shot in every expression, with talking and blinking, a faceset, and Ren'Py and Godot files. Shot of a character A character in any framing (full body to head), cut out, on white or in a scene. Barks Short lines for a character in idle, combat, hurt and victory; then translations. Base body A plain body (underwear, a bodysuit or a mannequin) that wardrobe pieces fit onto. Character Concept, turnaround, 3D, game mesh and a skeleton to review; then skin and clips. Retro sound effect Coins, jumps, lasers and explosions, made by a generator in a moment. Chiptune A chip-flavoured track from a description. To hear a track on real chip voices: Stems, MIDI, then add Chip render. Composed music A piece written by rules from a style and a seed, with a MIDI file for your DAW. Edit it bar by bar. Dialogue A scene of lines with stable keys, as a Godot Dialogue Manager file; then translations. Character model Your FBX, OBJ, GLB, VRM or .blend. A rigged humanoid gets clips straight away. Music file A track you have, at the project's loudness and era. Prop model Your own model as a prop's mesh, ready to texture, paint or export. Sound file A sound you have, finished like a made one (trim, era, loudness). Shader file A .gdshader you have, kept with its licence. Free texture Free voice Item text Name, descriptions and flavour text as checked JSON. Lore check Any text compared with your lore files: contradictions and unclear claims. Mesh from an image Your own picture of one object, turned into a low-poly model. Clip from a video Clip from a description Music A looping track at the project's loudness and sample rate. Names A list of names with meanings, in the style you describe. Pixel character A full-body character as true pixels. Pixel icon A UI or item icon, 32 px by default. Pixel sprite A prop, creature or object as true pixels with a limited palette. Pixel tiles A sheet of tiles cut at their borders, 16 or 32 px, with one palette. Prop From a prompt: concept art, a cut-out, then a low-poly model checked in Godot. Rig again Sound effect Round-robin variants of one sound, trimmed, levelled and given the target look's era. Shader A Godot shader written from your description, compiled in Godot until it works. Texture A seamless tile at the target look, with its maps and a Godot material. Effect Fire, smoke, sparks or magic: a sprite, then a flipbook animated by a video model. Voice A character's voice from a description, frozen as the reference for its lines. Wearable Armour, clothing or an accessory for a rigged character, fitted and skinned to it.

At a glance Kind body In New asset Characters & bodies → Base body Pipeline body, starting at Concept Review Rig Job file kind: body CLI gen run <job>.yaml A base body is a plain body that a wardrobe fits onto: underwear, a skin-tight bodysuit, or a smooth mannequin. It runs the character's steps, and its concept keeps the shapes clean: bare feet, short or tied-back hair, no accessories.

Pieces (wearables) made for the body are fitted onto it, each over the pieces on lower layers. Each piece records the body vertices it covers, and in Godot wardrobe.gd hides those while it's worn. Outfits are named sets of pieces: gen outfit <body> <name> <pieces…>.

Pick Mannequin for stylised games where skin never shows; Underwear when it does (swimwear, a bare-armed shirt). Long hair as a wardrobe piece (slot Hair) can be swapped like the rest. Make the inner layers first (shirt before coat): a piece is fitted over what exists when it's made.

At a glance Kind character In New asset Characters & bodies → 3D game character Pipeline character, starting at Concept Review Rig Job file kind: character CLI gen run <job>.yaml or gen make character "…" A character: concept art in an A-pose, four views, a 3D model, a game mesh, then a rig (skeleton and skin weights) and as many clips as you like.

The concept is worded for image-to-3D: an A-pose with the arms away from the body, open hands, hair in solid locks clear of the face. Turnaround draws the four views; Mesh builds from all four (Pixal3D multiview); Game mesh fits the budget; Rig (SkinTokens) makes the skeleton and weights in one pass, with bones named for Godot's humanoid profile. Long hair gets bone chains on the Rig step (Cloth: Auto).
Concept Turnaround High poly Game mesh Paint (optional) Rig Frame in 3D (optional) Then each clip: Motion

Keep held things out of the concept: a sword fused to a hand can't be rigged. Make it a prop. Review the rig with the test poses before making clips: fixing a joint later means redoing the clips' retarget. A whole cast in one style: keep the same project and wording ("stylised 3D game character").

Left and right swapped in the turnaround: the step warns; retake it. A joint in the wrong place: move it in the joint editor, then retake Rig with Keep the skeleton. Fingers fused: expected at low budgets; PS3 and PS4 keep more of them.

At a glance Kind composed_music In New asset Sound → Composed music Pipeline composed_music, starting at Compose Job file kind: composed_music CLI gen run <job>.yaml A piece written by rules and hand-written tables from a style and a seed, with no model: song.mid for your DAW and a preview to hear. Thirteen styles: Solo piano, Dark and calm, Solemn, Epic film, Film fantasy, Battle, Gentle town, Tense film, Chiptune, Jazz and lo-fi, Classical, Dark lament, and Bossa nova. The seed picks the whole plan: key, tempo, form, how the energy moves and the ending. An ending takes its time and comes home unless you pick Cut off or Open yourself. Edit it bar by bar with gen retake <asset> compose --set edit="reroll 5; lock 3": the new take keeps the seed and only the bars you name change. Other edits: reroll_rhythm, reroll_pitch, unlock, motif, insert, delete, give 5 auto C5:8,E5:8 (your own bar) and give_midi 5 file.mid. Bar ids are in the take's piece.json. Keep the take you like with gen promote. To build around your own tune, set Your tune: bars separated by |, like C5:8,E5:8 | G5:4,E5:4,D5:8 | - | IV F5:8,A5:8 (- is a bar for the composer to fill; a word before the notes is that bar's chord), or a .mid file in the project (4/4; the top notes are the tune). With Key on Auto the key comes from your notes, your bars are locked and the rest is written to fit them. The preview plays through GeneralUser GS, the same SoundFont as MIDI's previews. Its licence allows commercial use, but its author says he can't vouch for where every sample came from.

At a glance Kind prop In New asset Props & scenery → 3D prop Pipeline prop, starting at Concept Job file kind: prop CLI gen run <job>.yaml or gen make prop "…" A prop is any object that isn't a character: a still, a chair, a sword, a lantern. You describe it, and you get concept art, a 3D model, and a game-ready mesh in your target look's budget.

The concept is drawn as a single object at eye level on light grey, so it builds cleanly in 3D. Prep cuts it out; Mesh builds a dense model from the picture (Pixal3D or TRELLIS.2, by profile); Game mesh rebuilds it within the polygon and texture budget and bakes the texture; Paint can repaint it afterwards.

One object per prop: "a table with a lamp on it" makes one fused piece. Name the material and the wear: "weathered oak", "rusted iron bands". For a set of similar props, make one, then retake its Concept with a changed prompt.

At a glance Kind wearable In New asset Characters & bodies → Wearable Pipeline wearable, starting at Design Review Design Job file kind: wearable CLI gen run <job>.yaml A wearable is one piece of clothing, armour or an accessory, made for one rigged character or base body, fitted to its shape and skinned to its skeleton so it follows every animation.

Design redraws the character's own four renders wearing the piece (Qwen-Image-Edit) and cuts it out (SAM 3.1); the masks have to agree. Mesh builds it by one of three routes: follows the body (boots, gloves, shirts: made from the body's surface), rigid (helmets: built in 3D, then fitted), or hanging sheet (capes: the back view's outline hung behind the body with folds). Fit hugs it onto the body (and over lower layers) and pushes it out to the clearance; Paint colours it from the views; Wear copies the body's skin weights onto it, adds cloth chains for what hangs, and checks the poke in test poses and the swing in Godot.
In the app: New asset → Characters & bodies → Wearable. As a job file: asset: my_wearable kind: wearable prompt: …

One piece at a time: "leather boots", not "boots and gloves". The words choose the route and the slot: "boots" follows the body, "helmet" is rigid, "cape" hangs. Override with Route and Slot. Clearance is how far off the body it sits: raise it for thick materials and where the body pokes through.

The body pokes through at the knees or elbows: raise Clearance and run on from Fit; wear.json lists the poke per pose. A view shows the wrong piece: retake Design; the view that disagrees most is redrawn automatically once. A cape is too short: say the length ("a long cape down to the knees").

Field Type Default What it does Model model choice (WAI-Anima, NoobAI-XL) WAI-Anima Which model runs this step; an add-on extension can add more. Place prompt longtext The place in Danbooru tags: indoors, classroom, desks, window, afternoon; or outdoors, shrine, torii, forest, stone path. Nobody is drawn. Avoid negative text Tags to keep out, e.g. people, text. (advanced) Shape aspect choice (stage, wide, square) stage The picture's shape: VN stage (16:9) for scenes, Square for a portrait's background. Times of day times text evening, night The same scene again at: morning, day, evening, night, rain, snow (comma-separated; empty for none). Parallax layers parallax bool False A sky layer and a scene layer of each picture, for scrolling at different speeds.

Anima (WAI-Anima) (ultra_fast, fast, balanced, quality): A place with nobody in it, for visual novels and dialogue scenes; the same place again at other times of day keeps its layout. Structure: [no humans, scenery] (added for you) → [indoors or outdoors] → [the place] → [its objects] → [time and weather] → [light and mood]. Name the place and a few things in it: 'indoors, classroom, desks, window, chalkboard'. Time of day here is the first picture's; the Times of day field adds the others (evening, night, rain, snow) with the same layout. Wide shapes (VN stage, 16:9) suit scenery; Square is for portraits' backgrounds. Light words set the mood: 'warm lighting', 'sunbeams', 'moonlight', 'neon lights'. Parallax layers split the sky from the scene for scrolling. Avoid: People or characters: backgrounds are drawn empty so characters can go on top. Very busy prompts for small sizes: leave the model room. Examples: indoors, classroom, desks, window, chalkboard, afternoon, sunlight outdoors, shrine, torii, stone path, forest, summer, cicadas indoors, tavern, wooden tables, barrels, fireplace, warm lighting outdoors, fantasy town, market stalls, cobblestone street, day, blue sky NoobAI-XL (ultra_fast, fast, balanced, quality): A place with nobody in it, in NoobAI-XL's scenery tags; the same place at other times of day keeps its layout. Structure: [no humans, scenery] (added for you) → [indoors or outdoors] → [the place] → [its objects] → [time and weather] → [light]. Tag the place and a few things in it: 'indoors, classroom, desk, window, chalkboard'. Time of day is the first picture's; the Times of day field adds the others with the same layout. Light tags set the mood: 'sunlight', 'light rays', 'moonlight', 'neon lights'. Avoid: People: backgrounds are drawn empty. Sentences: NoobAI reads tags. Examples: indoors, classroom, desk, window, chalkboard, afternoon, sunlight outdoors, shrine, torii, stone path, forest, summer indoors, tavern, table, barrel, fireplace, warm lighting outdoors, town, market, stall, cobblestone, day, blue sky

Character prompt longtext Who they are, in Danbooru tags: 1girl or 1boy, hair, eyes, build, outfit (long black hair, red eyes, school uniform, red ribbon). Every shot reuses these tags; framing and background are added for you. Avoid negative text Tags to keep out of the sheet, e.g. hat, weapon. (advanced) Outfits outfits longtext Other outfits by name, one per line as name: tags (winter: winter coat, scarf, boots). A shot's Outfit adds one; the sheet wears the clothes in Character. (advanced)

Anima (WAI-Anima) (ultra_fast, fast, balanced, quality): The character's definition: a full-body sheet on white, front view, neutral. What you write here is the character's look; every shot of them reuses these tags (and their LoRA, once trained). Structure: [1girl / 1boy] → [species or role: elf, knight] → [hair: colour, length, style] → [eyes] → [marks: eyepatch, mole under mouth, scar] → [outfit, top to bottom] → [accessories]. Write only what's always true of the character: hair, eyes, marks, the default outfit. Poses, expressions and places belong in the Shot. List the outfit from top to bottom: 'white fur collar, burgundy vest, sleeveless, black belt, brown shorts, black gloves, brown thigh boots'. Plain tags, no weights: Anima holds a long list without them. Distinctive details (an eyepatch on one eye, a mole) are worth a word each; the LoRA learns them from the sheet. Make a few takes and use the cleanest: the sheet is what everything else copies. Avoid: Expressions and poses ('smiling, waving'): the sheet is neutral on purpose. A background: the sheet is drawn on white so it can be cut out and reused. Examples: 1girl, elf, pointy ears, very long blonde hair, black eyepatch, red eyes, mole under mouth, white fur collar, burgundy vest, sleeveless, grey turtleneck, black belt, dark brown shorts, black gloves, brown thigh boots 1boy, short messy black hair, green eyes, dark green hooded robe, brown belt, leather boots, holding a wooden staff 1girl, short silver hair, blue eyes, silver plate armor, blue cape, gauntlets, armored boots 1girl, long purple hair, yellow eyes, black witch hat, long black dress, red ribbon, brown boots NoobAI-XL (ultra_fast, fast, balanced, quality): The character's definition with NoobAI-XL: a full-body sheet on white, front view, neutral, in Danbooru tags. Every shot of the character reuses them (and their LoRA, once trained). Structure: [1girl / 1boy] → [a known character (series), if any] → [species or role] → [hair: colour, length, style] → [eyes] → [marks] → [outfit, top to bottom] → [accessories]. Danbooru tags, comma-separated, spaces not underscores: 'long hair, blonde hair, red eyes, eyepatch'. Only what's always true of the character; poses and expressions belong in the Shot. List the outfit top to bottom, one tag per garment: 'fur-trimmed collar, sleeveless jacket, turtleneck, belt, shorts, gloves, thigh boots'. NoobAI knows characters by their Danbooru names: 'frieren, sousou no frieren'. Weights are rarely needed; (tag:1.2) pushes one that keeps getting lost. Avoid: Sentences: NoobAI reads tags. Expressions, poses or a background: the sheet is neutral and on white. Quality tags (masterpiece, best quality): already added. Anima (WAI-Anima) (ultra_fast, fast, balanced, quality): A 2B anime model (Cosmos-Predict2 with a Qwen3 text encoder) trained on Danbooru. It reads Danbooru tags, plain sentences, or both mixed, and follows them much more closely than SDXL models: several characters, their outfits, who does what to whom. Structure: [how many: 1girl / 2girls / 1boy, 1girl] → [a known character and series] → [@artist] → [hair, eyes, outfit] → [expression, pose, action] → [framing: upper body, full body, cowboy shot] → [place, time, light]. Or two or more sentences saying the same. Tags are lowercase with spaces, not underscores: 'long hair, blue eyes, school uniform, smile'. Sentences work too, and mixing is fine: tags for the look, a sentence for what happens ('she laughs and points at the boy, who looks embarrassed'). Two characters: describe each one fully (hair, eyes, outfit), then what they do together. Names alone confuse it. An artist's style: '@name' (the @ matters; without it the effect is very weak). Weights need to be stronger than on SDXL models: (chibi:2) rather than (chibi:1.2). A very short prompt lets the model fill in a lot, sometimes more than you want; add detail, or 'safe' / 'nsfw' to say which. Ultra fast and Fast (Anima Turbo, 10 steps) are for trying ideas in seconds; Balanced and Quality use CFG, so Avoid works there. Quality adds a 1.5× Hires pass with the anime upscaler. Avoid: Quality tags yourself (masterpiece, best quality): they're already added. SDXL habits like piling up (tag:1.1) weights: they barely move Anima. Contradicting framing tags (portrait with full body). Examples: 1girl, solo, long silver hair, red eyes, black coat, gloves, serious, upper body, snowy forest, night, moonlight 1boy, solo, messy brown hair, green eyes, adventurer, leather armor, sword on back, smile, cowboy shot, fantasy town, market, day 2girls. the first girl has short pink hair in twintails and a frilled magical girl dress; the second has long black hair and a school uniform. they hold hands and laugh, full body, cherry blossoms, spring 1girl, solo, glasses, office lady, white shirt, pencil skirt, sitting at a desk with a computer, indoors, evening, window, city lights NoobAI-XL (ultra_fast, fast, balanced, quality): NoobAI-XL, the Model choice from the add-on: an Illustrious-based SDXL anime model trained on Danbooru and e621 tags. It follows comma-separated tags far better than sentences, knows thousands of characters, artists and outfits by their Danbooru names, and draws full scenes with backgrounds. Structure: [how many: 1girl, solo / 2boys] → [who: a known character (series)] → [hair, eyes, body] → [outfit] → [expression and pose] → [framing: upper body, full body, cowboy shot, portrait] → [place and time: classroom, sunset, rain] → [light and style: dramatic lighting, watercolor]. Use Danbooru tags, comma-separated: 'long hair, blue eyes, school uniform, smile'. Spaces, not underscores. Say how many people first: '1girl, solo', '1boy, 1girl', '2girls'. It decides the composition. Framing is a tag: 'portrait', 'upper body', 'cowboy shot' (thighs up), 'full body', 'from above', 'from side'. Known characters work by name and series: 'hatsune miku, vocaloid', 'frieren, sousou no frieren'. An artist's look comes from 'artist name' tags; use them sparingly, one or two. Weight a tag with (tag:1.2) to push it, (tag:0.8) to soften it. Backgrounds: describe the place in tags: 'indoors, classroom, window, sunlight, desk'. 'simple background, white background' for a plain one. Fast and Ultra fast (DMD2) are for trying ideas in seconds; Balanced and Quality use CFG, so Avoid works there and the drawing is cleaner. Quality adds a 1.5× Hires pass for detail. Avoid: Long sentences: NoobAI reads tags; a sentence becomes a jumble of half-matched tags. Quality tags yourself (masterpiece, best quality): they're already added. Contradicting framing tags (portrait with full body). At a glance Step id anime_rig2d Used by anime_rig2d Runs fast: SAM 3.1 parts Time 40–40 s VRAM 10 GB Extension gen.anime CLI gen retake <asset> anime_rig2d --set <field>=<value> Claude Code fields, retake, look, use A 2D cut-out rig of a transparent shot: parts on Godot bones (Skeleton2D and Polygon2D, no third-party runtime) with idle, sway and head-tilt animations.

SAM 3.1 finds the hair, face, arms, hands, sleeves and legs (each pair by looking twice); the torso is the rest. An arm or leg SAM finds alone is kept on its side; two legs touching as one piece stay with the torso. Ears, horns, a hat or a hair tuft (anything above the chin touching the face or hair) turn with the head. Limbs split at their middle; long hair below the chin is back hair, behind the body; short hair stays on the head and its ends swing on the hair bones. Joints come from the parts' shapes. Each part's hidden area is filled in smoothly so moving a limb shows no hole (checked at 15°), and the fill stays clear of the parts drawn behind it. Every part gets a grid mesh weighted to its bones. Godot plays each animation in the check; rig.json records the parts, bones, holes and the halo (the torso's fill showing round the head at ±8° in a colour that isn't the neck's), found.png shows what SAM found, and rig.webp plays the animations in the app.

App: open the asset and click 2D rig on the rail (or add it with the +), set the form on the left and press New take. Pick the take you like and press Use this take. Field Type Default What it does Shot shot asset A transparent Shot of a character, knee-up or full body, facing the viewer: split into hair, face, arms, legs and torso, each on its own bones.

Use a knee-up or full-body shot facing the viewer, arms at the sides, on Transparent. A shot on Plain white works, with a warning: its cut-out is rougher. Arms crossed or hands behind the back can't split into parts: the arms stay with the torso. In Godot, copy the whole take folder (or use Export to Godot, which copies it): the .tscn needs the part .pngs beside it, or the parts show as white shapes.
An arm missing from the parts: look at found.png; retake the shot with the arms clear of the body. The parts show white in Godot: the part .pngs aren't beside the .tscn; copy the whole take folder.

Expressions and actions go in Shot; the look is already in the character's tags. For a group, describe what they do together; draw a Layout with coloured boxes to place them. Anima (WAI-Anima) (ultra_fast, fast, balanced, quality): One shot of a defined character: their tags (and LoRA) come first, then what you write here. Expressions and actions are what the Shot is for: 'laughing, closed eyes, arms up', 'serious, holding sword, fighting stance'. An outfit change goes here too ('winter coat, scarf'); the character's usual outfit is already in their tags. With Background set to A scene, say the place here: 'tavern, indoors, warm lighting'. Pose choices in the form are written into the prompt for you; say finer details here ('left hand on hip'). Close framings (Chest-up, Head, Eyes) are drawn waist-up, then cropped around the face and given a detail pass. Avoid: Repeating the character's look: it's already in their tags. Framing tags: the Framing choice sets them. Framing, pose (an OpenPose skeleton with NoobAI) and background are choices in the form. Structure: [expression] → [action] → [outfit changes] → [place, when the background is a scene] → [light]. Expression and action tags: 'laughing, closed eyes, arms up', 'serious, holding sword, fighting stance'. With NoobAI the Pose choice is drawn from an OpenPose skeleton, so pose tags here are for details only ('hand on hip'). An outfit change goes here ('winter coat, scarf'); the usual outfit is already in the character's tags. With Background set to A scene, tag the place: 'tavern, indoors, warm lighting'. The seed picks the key, tempo, form, energy, ending and instruments. Form form choice (auto, aaba, abab, aab, takeover, calm, elegy, gather, answers, rise, pianoreward, journey, hearth, charge, duel, stroll, square, stalk, dread, stage, boss, head, loop, binary, rondo, lament, vigil) auto The piece's structure; each style has its own (the label says which). A climax is optional: Waves, A small swell, Steady and Calm have none. (advanced) Ending ending choice (auto, settle, broad, fade, long_fade, cut, open) auto Auto always takes time and resolves. Cut off and Open are abrupt or unresolved on purpose: for a game loop or a hard stop. (advanced) Key key choice (auto, 0, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9) auto The home note. (advanced) Tempo bpm int 0.0…200.0 0 Beats a minute; 0 lets the seed pick from the style's range. (advanced) Your tune tune text A whole tune to build around: |-separated bars, each C5:8,E5:8, IV C5:8,E5:8 (its chord), IV (a chord only) or - (free), or a .mid file in the project. With Key on Auto its key is read from the notes; its bars are locked and the rest is written to fit them. (advanced) Edit a bar edit text One or more edits, ;-separated, on the newest take, keeping its seed: reroll 5, reroll_rhythm 5, reroll_pitch 5, lock 3, unlock 3, motif 7, insert 5, delete 5, give 5 auto C5:8,E5:8 (your own bar), give_midi 5 file.mid; one instrument in a bar: reroll_part 5 kit, rework 5 nylon rhythm, give_part 5 kit 0:1:36,8:1:38; a part's channel: sound nylon 4, volume nylon -3, pan nylon -40. Bar ids are in piece.json. (advanced) Edit take edit_take int 0.0… 0 Which take an edit starts from; 0 is the newest. (advanced) Edit log edits text The edits this take was built with, in order. The piece is its seed plus this log: leave it alone unless you know the piece you want. (advanced)

Edit on a take opens the composer's editor. The strip on top is the piece: a chord card a bar, then a lane per instrument. Click an instrument's notes in a bar to work on that instrument there; click the chord card for the whole bar (Shift for a range). New idea is a fresh draw of what's picked; Rework rhythm and Rework pitches vary the notes already there, yours included. Each is a take, listed under Takes with the notes it changed lit: pick the one to keep, or go back to Current. A new idea for a whole bar asks first when the bar has notes of yours. Notes is the piano roll of the picked instrument (the kit is a step rack): click to draw, drag to move, drag an end to resize, right-drag erases. The bars either side are shown dimmed. Full screen gives the roll the lanes' room. The ruler over the strip works like a DAW's: click it to play from there (any beat), drag along it to mark a span that Play loops; a click clears the span. Picking a bar puts Play back at that bar. A line shows what's playing, and the view stays where you scroll it. With no span, the loop button repeats the picked bars. The − and + on a section's name remove or add a bar at its end. The side panel's channel gives the picked instrument another General MIDI sound (the kit: another drum kit), its volume and its pan. It keeps its part in the music: only how it's played changes. The side panel lists the chords that fit the picked bar, best first, with Set as motif, Insert after, Copy to and Delete. Nothing changes until Save as new take: it queues a Compose take from this take's seed and your edits, so the take you opened stays as it was.

Field Type Default What it does Prompt prompt longtext One subject, plainly described; the app adds the framing and background Enhance the prompt enhance bool False Gemma 4 rewrites the prompt in detail first (the rewrite is saved with the take) Control image control file Optional: a sketch, photo or render whose outline the concept follows (Fast) (advanced)

Say materials, colours and shapes; leave out camera and lighting words (they're added). Restyle (on a take) redraws it from the old one with a new description: the shape stays. Vary region redraws one part ("the helmet"). Z-Image-Turbo / FLUX.3 klein: props (fast, balanced): Alibaba's 6B few-step image model for one game object that becomes a 3D model. It reads plain sentences well and follows long, concrete descriptions; it has no negative prompt. Structure: [what it is] → [silhouette and proportions] → [parts and how they join] → [materials and finish] → [colours and wear] → [style]. Start with the silhouette: 'a squat barrel, wider in the middle', 'a tall narrow lantern'. The 3D steps rebuild the outline first. List the parts and how they connect: 'iron hoops nailed around oak staves', 'a ring handle riveted to the lid'. Name materials precisely: 'tarnished brass', 'split dark oak', 'chipped red enamel'. Wear makes it a game asset: 'scratched edges', 'rust in the seams', 'faded paint'. One object only. Things sitting on it (a candle on the chest) become part of the mesh. Avoid thin floating parts (chains, ropes, loose straps): image-to-3D merges or drops them. Say what you want instead of what you don't: there is no negative prompt. Style words set the era: 'low-poly PS1 game asset', 'hand-painted fantasy prop', 'clean 3D render'. Avoid: Scenes, rooms or several objects: the steps after concept want one subject alone. Camera, lighting and background words: they fight the framing the app adds. Text or logos on the object. Field Type Default What it does Style prompt longtext Comma-separated tags: genre, mood, instruments, tempo feel Length (seconds) duration float 5.0…240.0 60 How long the track is; a loop's length is matched to whole bars. BPM bpm int 40.0…240.0 100 Beats per minute; empty lets the model choose. Key keyscale text A minor The key, e.g. C major or A minor; empty lets the model choose. (advanced) Time signature timesignature choice (3, 4, 6) 4 Beats per bar: 4/4 for most game music, 3/4 for a waltz. (advanced) Lyrics lyrics longtext Section tags on their own lines ([verse], [chorus]); empty makes an instrumental (advanced) Seamless loop loop bool True Find a loop point and cut the track to it Era reverb reverb choice (default, on, off) default PS1 and PS2 add their console-style reverb by default; PS3 and PS4 leave it off (advanced)

Name the mood, instruments and tempo: "a calm village theme, acoustic guitar and flute, 90 bpm, loops". Length, BPM, Key and Time signature pin what the model would otherwise choose. Stems and MIDI come after, as manual steps. ACE-Step 1.5 (ultra_fast, fast): An open music model that takes two inputs: a caption of tags for the sound, and lyrics with section tags for the structure. Gen Studio makes instrumental loops by default. Structure: Comma-separated tags: [genre], [mood], [lead instruments], [rhythm and tempo feel], [production or era], [use]. Example: 'orchestral, heroic, brass and strings, steady march rhythm, cinematic, video game overworld'. Tags do the heavy lifting: be specific about genre, instruments and mood. Combine a few style tags for a more particular sound: 'chiptune, 8-bit, upbeat, arpeggios'. Name the instruments you want to hear: 'accordion', 'pizzicato strings', 'taiko drums', 'analog synth pad'. Describe the game use too: 'shop music', 'boss battle', 'calm village', 'dungeon ambience'. For instrumental music, keep lyrics as [Instrumental] (the default) and you can add 'instrumental, no vocals' to the tags. Set BPM and key in the fields rather than in the prompt; they are passed to the model directly. Loops: keep the style steady (no 'builds to a climax'): the loop finder needs matching start and end sections. If you add lyrics, use section tags on their own lines ([verse], [chorus], [bridge], [outro]) and 6-10 syllables per line. Avoid: Song or artist names: describe the sound instead. Long sentences about a story: the caption is about sound, not plot. Contradicting tags ('calm, aggressive'). Examples: calm harbour town, acoustic guitar, accordion, soft hand percussion, warm, folk, gentle sway, village theme heroic orchestral overworld, brass fanfare, strings, snare march, adventurous, cinematic, video game dark dungeon ambience, low drones, sparse piano, distant metallic hits, tense, slow, atmospheric chiptune, 8-bit, upbeat, fast arpeggios, square wave lead, retro platformer level ACE-Step 1.5 (lyrics) (ultra_fast, fast): ACE-Step sings the lyrics in the Style prompt's voice and genre; section tags set the song's structure. Empty makes an instrumental. Structure: Section tags on their own lines ([verse], [chorus], [bridge], [outro]), each followed by short lines of 6-10 syllables. Put each section tag on its own line: [intro], [verse], [chorus], [bridge], [outro]. Keep lines short, 6-10 syllables, and rhyme them in pairs. Repeat the chorus word for word: it makes the song's hook. Add a voice to the Style prompt (female vocals, male choir) to choose who sings. [Instrumental] alone makes a track without vocals. Avoid: Long lines: they get rushed or cut. Stage directions in the lyrics (sing softly): put the feel in the Style prompt. Lyrics on a loop: the loop finder needs matching sections, a song rarely has them. Examples: [verse] Lanterns burning by the shore Waiting for the ships once more [chorus] Raise the sails and sing along The sea will carry us home [verse] Iron gates and silent halls Shadows dancing on the walls [chorus] Hold the line, hold the light [verse] Snow is falling on the town Every roof in white and brown [chorus] Stay a while, stay a while

One object, seen straight on or at a slight angle. Bold colours and one detail: 32 px holds very little. For a set, keep the same wording and change the object; a fixed palette in Pixelate ties them together. Avoid: Words on the icon: no model draws readable text at this size. Scenes or several objects. The icon usually fills less of the frame; Pixelate crops to it. Structure: [the object], [its colour], [one distinguishing detail]. Try 48 px in Pixelate when the shading matters more than the crispness. Avoid: Words on the icon. Scenes or several objects. Field Type Default What it does Sprite prompt longtext One subject, plainly described: a small knight with a sword and shield. The pixel-art style and the plain background are added for you.

Z-Image-Turbo (pixel sprite) (ultra_fast, fast): The best of the installed models for pixel art: chunky, clean, readable sprites. Pixelate then turns the drawing into true pixels. Structure: [size and kind of subject], [one or two things it holds or wears], [main colours]. Example: 'a small knight with a sword and shield, silver armour, red plume'. One subject. Pixel art reads by silhouette: say what makes the shape. Name one or two strong colours: they become the palette's accents. A small, simple subject survives the shrink better than a detailed one. Details under a pixel or two vanish at 48 px: a belt buckle may, a sword won't. A new size or palette is a retake of Pixelate only, with no GPU; retake the drawing when the shape is wrong. Avoid: 'Four frames in a row' or 'sprite sheet': every model draws near-identical poses. Animation is not in this version. Backgrounds and scenes: Pixelate cuts around one subject on a flat background. Style words like 'pixel art', '16-bit' or 'white background': they are added for you. Examples: a small knight with a sword and shield, silver armour, red plume a green slime monster with big round eyes a wooden treasure chest with gold bands a red mushroom with white spots FLUX.3 klein (pixel sprite) (balanced): Draws convincing pixel art with finer shading, smaller in the frame; Pixelate crops to it. At 32 px its shading merges: stay at 48 or 64. Structure: [size and kind of subject], [what it holds or wears], [main colours]. Keep Pixelate at 48 px or more: its shading is finer than Z-Image's. Ask for clear colour blocks: 'silver armour, red plume' rather than textures. Avoid: Style words like 'pixel art' or 'white background': they are added for you. Examples: a small knight with a sword and shield, dark cloak, gold cross a red health potion bottle with a cork a little robot with a round head and antenna a brown bear standing Qwen-Image 2.1 (pixel sprite) (quality): The most faithful to a long description; its hatched shading can turn into busy pixels. Slower, and not better at pixel art than Z-Image. Structure: [subject], [details], [main colours]. Use it when a specific detail or combination matters: a blue tabard with a white star. Avoid: Style words: they are added for you. Textures and hatching: they become noise. Examples: a small knight with a sword and shield, silver armour, a blue tabard with a white star a chef with a tall hat holding a frying pan a mechanical owl with brass feathers a fox archer in a green hood

Light from: upper right, upper left, right, left or top. The light is white (a colour tint read ghostly in the tests). Strength 1–3: soft to bright. It isn't offered right after Rim light: FlowEdit and LightingRemap undo each other, so pick one of the two. Textures aren't relit.

Field Type Default What it does Model model choice (, WAI-Anima, Z-Image, Qwen-Image-Edit 2511, NoobAI-XL) Same as the picture: the model that drew it redraws the area (Z-Image for any other); Qwen-Image-Edit changes it by prompt. Area mask mask Draw the area to repaint (brush, lasso, box, or click with SAM 3.1). Nothing outside it changes. Strength strength float 0.05…1.0 0.5 How much the area may change: about 0.3-0.5 keeps its shape and colour (fixes, sketched colour), 0.5-0.7 reinterprets it, 1.0 draws it anew from what is around it. Prompt prompt longtext What the picture shows; filled in from the picture's own prompt. Say what the area should be if it should change. Find by name find text Or name the part ('the left hand', 'the helmet'): SAM 3.1 finds it and adds it to the area. Preset preset choice (none, hands, face) none Fix hands and Fix face find each hand or the face (SAM 3.1) and redraw each up close, at 0.5 and 0.4; the Area is not needed. Grow (px) grow int 0.0…64.0 8 How far past what you drew the repaint reaches. (advanced) Soft edge (px) blend int 0.0…64.0 16 How wide the edge that fades into the picture is (narrower at a low Strength). (advanced) Context context float 1.0…4.0 1.5 How much of the picture around the area the model sees, as a multiple of its size (at least 512 px); the crop is redrawn at 1024. (advanced) Match colour match_colour bool True Shifts the repaint's colours to the picture's, measured just around the area, so no patch shows. (advanced) The change change longtext What to do to the area, as an instruction: 'make the cape red', 'fix the left hand', 'remove the logo'.

Retouch: Redraw (Anima + Anima-LLLite inpaint) (ultra_fast, fast, balanced, quality): Repaints only the area you mark with the picture's own Anima model and the character's LoRA. The prompt is the picture's own tags, filled in for you. Structure: The picture's tags, then tags for the area: 'detailed hands, five fingers', 'open mouth, smile', 'red ribbon'. Quality tags are added for you. Low Strength (0.3-0.5) fixes detail in the same drawing; 0.6-0.8 redraws the part; 1.0 draws it anew from around it. Fix hands and Fix face find each hand or the face and redraw it up close: no drawing needed. Add the tag for the change at the end ('red ribbon', 'closed eyes'); keep the character's tags. Avoid: Natural-language sentences: Anima reads Danbooru tags best. Removing the character's own tags. Examples: 1girl, silver hair, detailed hands, five fingers 1girl, smile, open mouth, detailed face 1girl, closed eyes 1girl, red ribbon, hair ribbon Retouch: Redraw (Z-Image) (ultra_fast, fast, balanced, quality): Repaints only the area you mark. The prompt is the picture's own, filled in for you: keep it, and add what the area should be if it should change. Structure: The picture's prompt, then what the area should show: the subject, then the part in a few words ('… , her left hand open, five fingers'). Low Strength (0.3-0.5) keeps the shape and colour and fixes detail; 0.5-0.7 reinterprets; 1.0 draws it anew. To steer a colour or shape, paint a rough blob first (Edit in Krita) and redraw at about 0.4. Mark a little past the part: Grow and Soft edge blend it in, and nothing outside the mark changes. Not the result you wanted? Reroll for another seed, or Build on this take. Avoid: Describing a different picture: the area must still fit what is around it. Big areas at 1.0: make a new take instead. Examples: a knight in iron armour, his left hand in a leather glove a wooden chest with iron bands, a brass lock a red-haired archer, a detailed face, green eyes a stone tower, a small arched window Retouch: Change by prompt (Qwen-Image-Edit 2511) (ultra_fast, fast, balanced, quality): Changes the area you mark by an instruction. Qwen-Image-Edit sees the area and what is around it; only the marked area is pasted back. Structure: One instruction, verb first: what to do to the marked part ('make …', 'replace … with …', 'remove …', 'fix …'). Name the part as it is in the picture: 'the cape', 'the left glove', 'the sign'. One change at a time; Build on the take for the next one. Mark a little past the part, so the edge of the change blends in. Avoid: Long descriptions of the whole picture: say only the change. Changes reaching past the marked area: they are cut off at its edge. Examples: make the cape red fix the left hand: five fingers, relaxed replace the sword with a wooden staff remove the logo Retouch: Redraw (NoobAI-XL + inpainting ControlNet) (ultra_fast, fast, balanced, quality): Repaints only the area you mark with the picture's own NoobAI-XL model and the character's LoRA. The prompt is the picture's own tags, filled in for you. Structure: The picture's tags, then tags for the area: 'detailed hands, five fingers', 'open mouth, smile', 'red ribbon'. Quality tags are added for you. Low Strength (0.3-0.5) fixes detail in the same drawing; 0.6-0.8 redraws the part; 1.0 draws it anew from around it. Fix hands and Fix face find each hand or the face and redraw it up close: no drawing needed. Add the tag for the change at the end ('red ribbon', 'closed eyes'); keep the character's tags. Avoid: Natural-language sentences: NoobAI reads Danbooru tags best. Removing the character's own tags. Examples: 1girl, silver hair, detailed hands, five fingers 1girl, smile, open mouth, detailed face 1girl, closed eyes 1girl, red ribbon, hair ribbon

Describe the source and the action: "a thick potion bubbling in an iron cauldron, slow wet pops". Keep it to one event; layers come in the Effects step. PS1 and PS2 roll off the top and lower the sample rate on purpose. MOSS-SoundEffect v2 (fast): OpenMOSS's 1.3B flow-matching model at 48 kHz: environments, creatures, human actions and short percussive sounds, up to 30 s. It reads full natural sentences. Structure: One plain sentence: [what makes the sound] [doing what] [where, how close], plus any detail of timing ('twice', 'then fades'). Write a natural sentence: 'A large dog barks twice in an empty courtyard.' Timing words work: 'twice', 'slowly', 'then silence', 'building up'. Name the place for the acoustics: 'in a stone cellar', 'in an open field'. Creatures and ambiences are this model's strength; it also handles human actions. It makes up to 30 s: use Fast for long ambiences (Woosh, at Balanced and Quality, makes up to 5 s). English or Chinese prompts both work. Avoid: Music, singing or speech. Lists of tags: this model was trained on captions. Examples: A large dog barks twice in an empty stone courtyard. A wooden door slams shut in a small room. A crowd of goblins chatters and cackles in a cave. Waves crash on rocks at night, with wind. Stable Audio 3 Small-SFX (ultra_fast): Stability AI's small sound-effects model, distilled to 8 steps: very fast one-shots and short loops. It follows short, concrete descriptions. Structure: [source], [action], [material or size], [recording: close or distant, dry or roomy]. A category word first helps: 'Footstep:', 'Impact:', 'UI:'. Name the source and the action: 'a sword is drawn from a leather scabbard'. Give material and size: 'small glass bottle', 'heavy iron gate'. Say how it was recorded: 'close-up, dry' for game one-shots; 'distant, echoing' for ambience. Keep the length short for one-shots (0.5–3 s); use 10–30 s for ambience loops. Ask for one event: 'a single footstep' beats 'footsteps' when you want one-shots. Use Variants for round robin: the same sound several times, slightly different each time. Avoid: Music or melodies: use the Music asset. Speech or words: use Voice. Several unrelated events in one prompt. Examples: Footstep: a single boot step on wet stone, close-up, dry Impact: a wooden sword hits a wooden shield, close-up UI: a soft, bright menu click, short A small glass potion bottle is uncorked with a pop Woosh (balanced, quality): Sony AI's sound-effect foundation model at 48 kHz, up to 5 s: DFlow (distilled, a few steps) at Balanced, Flow (adaptive solver, the best quality) at Quality. Trained on sound-effect libraries, so it reads short captions. Its licence is non-commercial, and that covers what it makes. Structure: A short caption: [the source] [the action] [a quality or place], e.g. 'sportscar engine revving and driving away quickly'. Short captions work best: 'heavy wooden door creaking open slowly'. Name the material and the action: 'glass bottle shattering on concrete'. Add how it moves or ends: 'whoosh passing left to right', 'impact with a long tail'. Keep it to one event: Woosh makes up to 5 s. Make a Fast take (MOSS) too and use Compare to pick between them. Avoid: Music, singing or speech. More than 5 s: use Fast (MOSS, up to 30 s) for long ambiences. Commercial releases: Woosh's outputs are CC-BY-NC. Examples: sportscar engine revving and driving away quickly heavy wooden door creaking open slowly sword whoosh, fast swing glass bottle shattering on concrete

Fast runs Gemma 4 26B; Balanced and Quality Gemma 4 31B with up to eight judge rounds. Each round gets the notes of the rounds before, and is told when a fix rendered pixel-identical. A score of 7 or more is accepted. judge.json keeps every round's score and notes, judge/N.png its preview. Field Type Default What it does Describe the shader prompt longtext What it looks like and where it goes: a 3D surface (lava with glowing cracks), a 2D sprite effect (a dissolve), or a sky. Say where it's used (a 2D sprite, a 3D mesh, the sky) and what moves. Name the parameters you want to tweak ("with a uniform for the edge colour"). Shader writer (Gemma 4 + Godot compile loop) (quality, balanced, fast, ultra_fast): A general text model (Gemma 4 31B at Balanced and Quality) writes Godot 4 shading language from your description; Godot compiles it and the errors go back until it compiles. Then the model looks at a render of it, scores it and fixes what's missing, keeping the best round. Describe the look in concrete terms: that is what it checks. Structure: [where it goes: a 3D surface, a 2D sprite or UI, a sky] → [what it looks like] → [how it moves] → [what should be tweakable]. Say the target first: '3D surface', 'a 2D sprite effect', 'a sky'. It sets shader_type. Describe the look in shapes and colours: 'dark crust with thin glowing orange cracks'. Say how it moves: 'pulses every two seconds', 'scrolls left slowly', 'flickers'. Name the knobs you want: 'tweakable glow colour and crack width' become uniforms. Keep one effect per shader; combine them in Godot with next_pass or several materials. If the look is off, read judge.json in the take (what it saw, its score) and retake with a more concrete description. Avoid: GLSL or Shadertoy terms (iTime, fragColor): ask for the effect, not a port. Several unrelated effects in one shader. Examples: a 3D lava surface: dark crust with glowing orange cracks that pulse slowly; tweakable glow colour and crack width a 2D dissolve for sprites with a glowing edge, driven by a 0-1 progress uniform a 3D water surface with gentle waves and a foam line where it meets objects a toon shader for characters: two light bands, a rim light and a tweakable shadow colour

Field Type Default What it does Describe the motion prompt longtext One person, the body's movement, in order Length (seconds) duration float 1.0…10.0 3 How long the clip is. Frame rate fps choice (15, 30, source) Source keeps the motion's own rate Keys stepped bool Stepped keys hold each pose (the PS1 look) Static pose pose bool False One held pose instead of a motion (describe the pose): for Frame in 3D, or a pose for your game

One action per clip: "a confident walk cycle", "a two-handed sword swing". Clips loop and stay in place by default. A job file can set loop: false and in_place: false; the app's form has neither yet. HY-Motion 1.0 (balanced, quality): Tencent's billion-parameter motion model (Lite on Balanced, full on Quality). It turns an English description of one person's movement into a clip; Balanced keeps clips under 5 seconds. Structure: 'A person' + the body action + how + simple steps in order: 'A person walks forward confidently, turns left, and keeps walking with arms swinging.' Write in English and keep it under 60 words (under 30 on Balanced). Describe one person and the body's movement, in the order it happens. Add manner words: slowly, cautiously, limping, energetic, tired. Name the limbs when it matters: 'swings a sword overhead with both hands'. For a game loop (walk, idle, run), describe one steady action without a start or end pose. Short, single-action clips retarget and loop best; chain actions only when you need them. Avoid: Props and scenery the motion can't show (the model makes body movement only). Several people or interactions with another character. Camera directions. Examples: A person walks forward at a steady pace with arms swinging naturally. A person stands idle, breathing and shifting weight from one foot to the other. A person jogs forward with a relaxed, even stride. A person swings a sword overhead with both hands and strikes down. MoMask (fast): A masked-transformer motion model trained on HumanML3D. It knows everyday motions described in short, plain sentences. Structure: HumanML3D style: 'A person' / 'Someone' + one action + an optional detail: 'A person walks in a clockwise circle and stops where he began.' Start with 'A person' or 'Someone', as the training captions do. One plain sentence, one or two actions. Everyday motions work best: walking, running, jumping, sitting, waving, kicking, dancing. Add direction and counts when they matter: 'takes four steps backwards', 'turns around'. Name the side: 'kicks with the right leg', 'raises the left arm'. Avoid: Rare or acrobatic moves the dataset barely covers (it may fall back to walking). Long multi-step stories. Objects and scenery. Examples: A person is walking slowly. A person jogs forward. A person stands still and looks around. Someone is doing jumping jacks. Quaternius animation library (ultra_fast): Not a generator: it picks the best-matching clip from Quaternius' Universal Animation Library (46 hand-made, CC0 animations) by the words in your prompt. Structure: A few keywords naming the action: 'walk', 'jog forward', 'idle', 'punch', 'death', 'sitting', 'dance', 'crouch', 'roll', 'jump'. Use the action word: walk, jog or run, idle, jump, punch, shoot, roll, crouch, dance, sit, death, pick up, talk. Add 'forward' to prefer a forward-moving clip. Words like walking, runs and dies are understood (they map to walk, jog and death). A prompt with no matching word gets the idle loop. Clips ending in Loop are preferred on ties, which suits game cycles. Avoid: Descriptions of style or emotion: only action words count. Anything not in the library (climbing a ladder, swimming): pick Fast or Balanced for those. Examples: walk jog forward idle jump

The app asks for a flat, evenly lit, tiling surface Palette colours choice (16, 256, full) Empty: the target look decides (PS1 16, PS2 256, PS3 and PS4 full colour) (advanced) Dither dither bool Bake a 4×4 ordered dither into the palette (the PS1 look). Left unset: drawn large and resized down smoothly, as before. (advanced)

Z-Image-Turbo (fast): Alibaba's 6B few-step image model. Rich, photographic surfaces; describe the material in plain sentences. No negative prompt. Structure: [material], [its parts or pattern], [colours], [wear and age], [style]. One or two plain sentences. Describe a surface, not an object: 'mossy cobblestones', not 'a cobblestone street'. Name the pattern's scale: 'small square tiles', 'large irregular flagstones', 'fine wood grain'. Even, repeating detail tiles best; one big feature (a crack across the middle) repeats visibly. Say the wear: 'chipped paint', 'rust streaks', 'polished by feet'. A style word sets the era: 'hand-painted', 'photo-sourced', 'pixel-art-like PS1 texture'. For PS1 and PS2 the app reduces the colours afterwards; strong, simple colour areas survive that best. Retake with the dice before rewriting: seams and layout vary a lot between seeds. Avoid: Perspective words (a corridor, a horizon, 'looking down the road'): textures are flat and straight-on. Lighting directions or cast shadows: baked-in light breaks when the texture is lit in the game. Single centred objects: they repeat as a grid of copies. Examples: Old cobblestones of uneven grey granite, moss in the gaps, worn smooth, photo-sourced game texture Weathered wooden planks running horizontally, dark knots, faded green paint flaking off Rusted iron plate with rivets in a regular grid, orange rust streaks over dark steel Red clay roof tiles in overlapping rows, a few chipped, sun-faded SDXL + DMD2 (4 steps) (ultra_fast): Stable Diffusion XL distilled to 4 steps. Very fast, and SDXL makes the most regular, tile-friendly surfaces. It runs at CFG 1, so the negative prompt barely matters. Structure: Short comma-separated phrases, material first: [material], [pattern], [colours], [wear], [style], 'texture'. Put the material first and end with 'texture' or 'seamless texture'. Short phrases, not sentences: CLIP reads about 75 tokens. Regular patterns (bricks, tiles, planks, weave) come out best. Colour and wear words work well: 'mossy', 'rusty', 'faded blue', 'polished'. The app adds the flat, even, straight-on framing; leave camera words out. Avoid: Text, signs or lettering: SDXL draws garbled letters. Scenes and objects: a texture is a surface. Examples: grey cobblestones, moss between stones, worn, game texture wooden planks, horizontal, dark knots, flaking green paint, texture rusty iron plate, rivet grid, orange rust streaks, texture red clay roof tiles, overlapping rows, sun-faded, texture
