Field Type Default What it does What it sounds like sound_prompt longtext Optional: words to steer it ('a fiery whoosh, crackling embers'); empty uses the effect's own prompt Variants variants int 1.0…8.0 3 How many versions of the sound to make (a round robin). (advanced)

Woosh video-to-audio (effect sound) (ultra_fast): Woosh's video-to-audio model (DVFlow, 8 s) hears the animated effect's frames and times the sound to them; these words only steer what it sounds like. Empty: the effect's own prompt is used. Structure: A short caption of the sound, not the picture: [the source or material] [the action] [a quality], e.g. 'a fiery whoosh, crackling embers'. Describe what you hear, not what you see: 'electric crackle and hum', not 'blue lightning'. Name the material: fire, ice, water, stone, metal, energy. Say how it starts and ends: 'a sharp burst, then a hissing tail'. Leave timing to the frames: the model follows the effect's motion. Keep it short: a few words beat a sentence. Avoid: Music, singing or speech. Visual words (colours, shapes, glow): they don't make a sound. Several unrelated sounds: one effect, one sound. Examples: a fiery whoosh, crackling embers electric crackle and buzzing hum icy shatter with a glassy tinkle deep magical boom, rumbling tail

Claude Code: fields shows the form, retake makes a take, look shows it, use picks it.

Field Type Default What it does The voice prompt longtext 40-80 words: age, gender, pitch, accent, pace, texture, mood and how they speak Sample line sample longtext What the reference clip says (a varied sentence clones best); empty uses a stock line (advanced) Language language choice (English, Japanese, Chinese, Korean, German, French, Russian, Portuguese, Spanish, Italian) English The language the voice speaks.

Qwen3-TTS VoiceDesign (ultra_fast, fast): Qwen's 1.7B voice designer: it speaks the sample line in a voice made from your description, and that clip becomes the character's frozen voice for every dialogue line. 40 to 80 words work best. Structure: Who they are (age, gender, role), then the voice itself: pitch, texture (gravelly, breathy, clear), accent, pace and rhythm, then the mood and how they talk to people. Write 40-80 words: shorter descriptions give generic voices, much longer ones get ignored. Give an age and a gender first: 'A woman in her sixties', 'a boy of about twelve'. Name the texture: gravelly, husky, breathy, nasal, bright, warm, thin, booming. Pitch and pace are separate: 'low-pitched and slow', 'high and quick'. An accent works as a broad region: 'a soft Irish accent', 'a crisp upper-class English accent'. Say how they talk to people: 'patient, as if explaining to a child', 'clipped, giving orders'. One mood, not three: the voice is frozen, so a range of emotions blurs it. The Language field sets the language; describe the voice in English either way. Avoid: Real people's names ('sounds like a famous actor'): describe the voice instead. What the character says or their backstory: only how they sound matters here. Effects (robotic, echo, radio): the era effects come later in the chain. Contradictions ('deep, high-pitched voice'). Examples: An old lighthouse keeper in his seventies, deep and gravelly baritone, slow and deliberate, a soft coastal accent, tired but kind, every sentence trailing off a little as if he is half lost in memories, speaking quietly to someone he trusts. A young woman of about twenty, a bright clear mezzo voice, quick and confident, a light American accent, cheerful and teasing, she speaks with a smile and lifts the ends of her sentences as if everything is a small adventure. A battle-worn knight commander in her forties, low and firm alto with a slight rasp, measured pace, a crisp northern English accent, stern but fair, she gives orders in short sentences and never raises her voice. A nervous goblin merchant, a thin reedy tenor that cracks when excited, very fast with sudden pauses, a sly wheedling tone, always trying to sell something, laughing nervously between words.

Field Type Default What it does The piece prompt longtext What to wear, as you'd describe it: leather boots, a steel chestplate, a wool hood. One piece at a time. Character character text The character asset (it needs its Rig step). Slot slot choice (auto, head, hair, face, neck, torso_inner, torso_outer, hands, waist, legs, feet, back, accessory) auto Where it goes in the character's wardrobe: one piece per slot and layer is worn at a time. Cloth material cloth_material choice (auto, cloth, leather, hair, chain) auto How it swings: stiffness, drag and gravity for Godot's spring bones. (advanced)

This step's form holds the whole wearable's settings: Slot, Layer, Route, Clearance, Cloth. Review the four views before running on: what's drawn here is what gets built. Wearable design (Qwen-Image 2.1 on the character's renders) (ultra_fast, fast, balanced, quality): Your character, rendered from four sides, is redrawn wearing the piece you describe; SAM 3.1 then finds the piece in each view by the same words, so describe it as a thing you could point at. Structure: [material and colour] → [what it is] → [length or coverage] → [one or two details]. Name one piece: 'brown leather boots', 'a steel chestplate', 'a red wool hood'. Several at once confuse the cut-out. Say how much it covers: 'knee high', 'ankle boots', 'a breastplate down to the waist'. Materials read well: leather, steel, wool, cloth, fur, gold trim. Keep it close to the body: capes, long skirts and wings need cloth simulation (not fitted yet). If SAM misses it in a view, retake with plainer words ('boots' rather than 'sabatons'). Avoid: Loose or floating parts (capes, scarves blowing, wings). Changing the character itself (hair, face): only the piece is kept. Examples: brown leather boots, knee high a steel chestplate with rivets a red wool hood leather gloves

At a glance Step id wear_mesh Used by wearable Runs built into the core (no model) Extension gen.core CLI gen retake <asset> wear_mesh --set <field>=<value> Claude Code fields, retake, look, use Builds the wearable's 3D shape by one of three routes, chosen by its words (or the Route field).

Follows the body (boots, gloves, shirts, trousers): the body's own faces inside the four masks' hull, offset by the clearance and a thickness, joined into one closed shell. It fits by construction, and leaves room over lower layers. Rigid (helmets, pauldrons, belts): Pixal3D builds it from the four views; Fit then hugs it to the body. Hanging sheet (capes): the back view's outline (filled in where the body's armour hid it) hung behind the body like a string pulled down, with folds deepening towards the hem. mesh.json records the route, why, and the pieces it was fitted over.
